#20935. NEGATE: Constrained Semantic Guidance for Linguistic Negation in Text-to-Video Diffusion

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (190 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

NEGATE: Constrained Semantic Guidance for Linguistic Negation in Text-to-Video Diffusion

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (190 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2603.06533v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Negation is a fundamental linguistic operator, yet it remains inadequately modeled in vision-language generation systems. In this work, we present a formal treatment of linguistic negation in vision-language models by modeling it as a structured feasibility constraint on semantic guidance within diffusion dynamics. Rather than introducing heuristics or retraining model parameters, we reinterpret classifier-free guidance as defining a semantic enhancement direction and enforce negation by projecting the update onto a convex constraint set derived from linguistic structure. This formulation provides a unified framework for handling diverse negation phenomena, including object absence, graded non-inversion semantics, multi-negation composition, and scope-sensitive disambiguation. Our approach is training-free, compatible with pretrained diffusion backbones, and defined on the classifier-free guidance update, which lets it operate over temporally evolving video trajectories. In addition, we introduce a structured negation-centric benchmark suite that isolates distinct linguistic failure modes in generative systems, to further research in this area. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves robust negation compliance while preserving visual fidelity and structural coherence, moving the treatment of linguistic negation in generative vision-language models beyond representation-level evaluation.

#20934. Exact and Approximate Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Multivariate Diffusions under High-Frequency Sampling

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (235 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Exact and Approximate Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Multivariate Diffusions under High-Frequency Sampling

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (235 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22675v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish the asymptotic theory of the exact maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for discretely observed multivariate ergodic diffusions under high-frequency, long-span sampling, solving an open problem posed by \citet{YCW2019} and \citet{Li2013}. The drift may grow linearly, and the volatility is bounded away from zero and either bounded or proportional to $1+|x|$. When the sampling interval decays polynomially, the exact MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient, with rates $\sqrt{n\Delta_n}$ for drift and $\sqrt n$ for diffusion parameters. Under an additional condition on ergodic averages, and when the time span $n\Delta_n$ also grows polynomially, its moments converge as well. The proof never analyzes the exact likelihood directly: it indicates that a closed-form density expansion of sufficiently high order is uniformly accurate in relative terms at every observed transition, so that the two log-likelihoods differ by $o_P(1)$ uniformly in the parameter. The same argument yields accuracy conditions under which an approximate likelihood is asymptotically equivalent to the exact one; in particular, the approximate MLE of Yang, Chen and Wan converges to the true parameter. For the delta-expansion estimator of fixed order $K\ge1$, we derive the leading bias explicitly. It shows that $n\Delta_n^{K+1}\to0$ cannot be weakened when the bias constant is nonzero, and that the bias falls on the drift parameters for even $K$ and on the diffusion parameters for odd $K$. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the predicted biases.

The Memory Trust Gap: Reliance on Stale Evidence Across Model Scales in LLM Agents

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (182 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2609.01852v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Persistent-memory agents can follow stale information despite current authoritative evidence. We study stale-evidence reliance across Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B checkpoints using two controlled, action-scored suites: a Benefit suite requiring stored information and a Safety suite providing current evidence as static prompt text. We distinguish stale-value reliance from net accuracy loss relative to no memory. Benefit-suite reliance is 0.92-1.00 across checkpoints. In the Safety suite, larger checkpoints resist a plain stale note but incur substantial harm when it appears newer. A full $2\times2\times2\times2$ factorial manipulates label, recency, source authority, and position. Direct cross-size contrasts identify stronger recency effects in the larger tested checkpoints and a position-effect sign reversal within Qwen3. Metadata improves accuracy at all four checkpoints, with larger gains at 4B/8B; pre-resolution yields near-ceiling accuracy across all four. Llama-Instruct comparisons provide cross-family evidence for selected effects, while RGB and MisBench corroborate stale-value reliance. A framing control shows that the failure extends beyond memory-labeled content. These results characterize cue-dependent vulnerability across tested checkpoints without isolating capability or evaluating a complete memory lifecycle.

arXiv:2611.21057v2 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Similar tactile contacts can call for different corrections depending on the configuration of the hand, object and target. Rather than supplying touch and wrist vision separately, fusing them before policy injection better grounds tactile features in visual context, yielding more accurate contact representations. We introduce Wrist-Informed Tactile Representations (WiTac), a pretrained encoder that learns such representations before action generation. Pretrained on nearly 300 hours of SharpaDex data, WiTac deeply fuses tactile signals with hand motion and wrist views into a comprehensive contact representation. Conditioning downstream VLA policies (GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$) on WiTac substantially improves task success over vision-only base policies across four contact-rich manipulation tasks (+28.8% and +15.0% on average), and further outperforms a wrist-free tactile encoder by 18.8% and 7.5%, respectively. Offline analyses further show that incorporating wrist vision yields more accurate contact descriptors, stronger joint task-contact discrimination, greater feature stability under tactile noise, and clearer action-direction readout from similar contacts. Project page: https://wrist-informed-tactile-representations.github.io/.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2601.21760v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Climate downscaling of General Circulation Models (GCMs) is an ill-posed inverse problem, as GCM outputs and reanalysis fields arise from different dynamical systems and lack fine-scale temporal pairing. Supervised methods thus rely on synthetic degradations or model-specific adaptation, limiting generalization across heterogeneous GCMs. Zero-shot diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) avoids paired supervision by combining a high-resolution climate prior with inference-time constraints from coarse GCM inputs, but faces consistency and efficiency challenges. We propose GCM-consistent Diffusion for Zero-shot Downscaling (GCD), which addresses these challenges with geographic conditioning, spectrally filtered measurement guidance, and distillation-accelerated Conjugate Gradient guidance. GCD reduces inference from 1,000 diffusion steps to 6 while maintaining consistency with the coarse GCM inputs. Across five heterogeneous GCMs, GCD achieves competitive 99th-percentile extreme-event accuracy and reconstructs plausible high-frequency tropical cyclone structures without model-specific retraining. Github: https://github.com/shawnvonbohr/GCD-Climate-Downscaling.git.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Cross-Epoch Bias in SGD-based Leave-One-Out Influence: Analysis and Accumulative Correction

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (248 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2510.26185v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Training-data influence estimates support data selection and cleansing by predicting the effects of removing individual examples. The standard multi-epoch SGD-Influence Estimator (SGD-IE) aggregates contributions from a sample's repeated appearances along the recorded trajectory. When used to approximate finite deletion, it omits an interaction: later removals act on the parameter displacement accumulated from earlier removals. We introduce the Accumulative SGD-Influence Estimator (ACC-SGD-IE) to account for how earlier removals change the effect of removing the same sample again. It uses the sample's Hessian at subsequent appearances to correct the estimated parameter change. Our non-convex analysis shows that this correction removes SGD-IE's additional interaction contribution from the finite-horizon error bound: the omitted interaction produces a local error linear in the accumulated parameter change, while the remaining Taylor remainder is bounded quadratically under Lipschitz-Hessian assumptions. The bounds characterize how training propagates the remaining error. In non-convex experiments across clean and noisy tabular, text, and vision datasets, ACC-SGD-IE reduces validation-loss-change RMSE by 10.8% and improves Jaccard@10% by 15.2% on average relative to SGD-IE. These gains also translate into lower test misclassification rates after data cleansing on MNIST and CIFAR10 at the evaluated removal budgets. On noisy industrial datasets, it reduces aggregate parameter RMS error with a mean relative reduction of 53.4%. We further discuss computational tradeoffs, provide complementary theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation for strongly convex objectives, and explore potential extensions of the accumulative correction mechanism to other influence estimators.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2602.19202v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Event cameras excel at high-speed, low-power, and high-dynamic-range scene perception. However, as they fundamentally record only relative intensity changes rather than absolute intensity, the resulting data streams suffer from a significant loss of spatial information and static texture details. In this paper, we address this limitation by leveraging the generative prior of a pre-trained video diffusion model to reconstruct high-fidelity video frames from sparse event data. Specifically, we first establish a baseline model by directly applying event data as a condition to synthesize videos. Then, based on the physical correlation between the event stream and video frames, we further introduce the event-based inter-frame residual guidance to enhance the accuracy of video frame reconstruction. Furthermore, we extend our method to video frame interpolation and prediction in a zero-shot manner by modulating the reverse diffusion sampling process, thereby creating a unified event-to-frame reconstruction framework. Experimental results on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms previous reconstruction approaches on most quantitative metrics and achieves superior qualitative results, while achieving competitive zero-shot performance compared with dedicated methods explicitly trained for interpolation and prediction tasks. We also refer the reviewers to the video demo contained in the supplementary material for video results. The code will be publicly available at https://github.com/CS-GangXu/UniE2F.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Optimal Network Design under Node Failures

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (249 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.21856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Networks are frequently constructed before it is determined which nodes will persist. We address the design problem in scenarios where nodes fail independently, links are costly and must be established in advance, and the benefits to surviving nodes diminish with distance. Examples include supplier, interbank, and infrastructure networks. Among all possible networks, the complete, star, and empty configurations are each welfare-optimal within specific ranges of link costs. However, with four or more nodes, failures introduce a range of costs in which every optimal network contains more links than the star but fewer than the complete network. At the lower end of this range, we show that the optimal networks are exactly those obtained by removing a matching from the complete network. We develop an exact algorithm for complete multipartite networks. It finds an optimal network by dynamic programming in a number of operations that grows with the fourth power of the number of nodes, although the class itself grows superpolynomially. For networks with up to six nodes, restricting the design to this class results in no loss under explicit conditions. We also characterize pairwise-stable networks within this class and establish their existence for every level of link cost. Finally, we quantify the cost of misjudging failure risk. Overestimating node survival leads to overbuilding and can yield lower welfare than building nothing, whereas underestimating it never does. Under uncertain failure risk, design should therefore favor conservative reliability estimates.

#20924. Nested logit: model structure and normalisation

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (234 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Nested logit: model structure and normalisation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (234 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22638v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nested logit remains a widely used model, especially in applied work. However, there remains substantial confusion surrounding the existence of different versions of the model, different normalisations for the same version, and different software implementations. This paper argues that the labels in common use, RU1 and RU2, and the name non-normalised nested logit (NNNL) itself, have contributed to the confusion. The model is written in two forms: one in which utilities are divided by the structural parameter of the nest that contains them, which is consistent with utility maximisation by construction, and one without that division, known as NNNL. The difference between these forms is not one of normalisation. Normalising at the top or at the bottom gives the same model, and NNNL is itself normalised. What distinguishes the forms is whether the division is performed. In short, normalisation changes the units, whereas division changes the model. The undivided form coincides with the utility-consistent one only under specific conditions, and otherwise is consistent with utility maximisation only under utilities other than those specified, in which generic coefficients become nest-specific. The paper highlights that RU1 has been used for three different specifications, compares how widely used software packages normalise and report their parameters, and illustrates the consequences with calculated examples. The recommendation is that models be described by what they do, rather than by these labels.

arXiv:2510.19244v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) achieves remarkable performance but lacks interpretability, limiting trust in policy behavior. The existing SILVER framework (Li, Siddique, and Cao 2025) explains RL policy via Shapley-based regression but remains restricted to low-dimensional, binary-action domains. We propose SILVER with RL-guided labeling, an enhanced variant that extends SILVER to multi-action and high-dimensional environments by incorporating the RL policy's own action outputs into the boundary points identification. Our method first extracts compact feature representations from image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution, and then employs RL-guided labeling to generate behaviorally consistent boundary datasets. Surrogate models, such as decision trees and regression-based functions, are subsequently trained to interpret RL policy's decision structure. We evaluate the proposed framework on two Atari environments using three deep RL algorithms and conduct human-subject study to assess the clarity and trustworthiness of the derived interpretable policy. Results show that our approach maintains competitive task performance while substantially improving transparency and human understanding of agent behavior. This work advances explainable RL by transforming SILVER into a scalable and behavior-aware framework for interpreting deep RL agents in high-dimensional, multi-action settings.

CORE: Concept-Oriented Reinforcement for Bridging the Definition-Application Gap in Mathematical Reasoning

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (211 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Sources indicate that arXiv:2512.18857v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often solve challenging math exercises yet fail to apply the concept right when the problem requires genuine understanding. Popular Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) pipelines reinforce final answers but provide little fine-grained conceptual signal, so models improve at pattern reuse rather than conceptual applications. We introduce CORE (Concept-Oriented REinforcement), an RL training framework that turns explicit concepts into a controllable supervision signal. Starting from a high-quality, low-contamination textbook resource that links verifiable exercises to concise concept descriptions, we run a sanity probe showing LLMs can restate definitions but fail concept-linked quizzes, quantifying the conceptual reasoning gap. CORE then (i) synthesizes concept-aligned quizzes, (ii) injects brief concept snippets during rollouts to elicit concept-primed trajectories, and (iii) reinforces conceptual reasoning via trajectory replacement after group failures, a lightweight forward-KL constraint that aligns unguided with concept-primed policies, or standard GRPO directly on concept-aligned quizzes. Across several models, CORE delivers consistent gains over vanilla and SFT baselines on both in-domain concept-exercise suites and diverse out-of-domain math benchmarks. CORE unifies direct training on concept-aligned quizzes and concept-injected rollouts under outcome regularization. It provides fine-grained conceptual supervision that bridges problem-solving competence and genuine conceptual reasoning, while remaining algorithm- and verifier-agnostic.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.21035v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Autonomous monitoring and intervention in semi-structured agricultural environments, such as orchards and vineyards, require mobile robots to navigate to locations across diverse field configurations. This entails performing navigation behaviors including in-row driving, row turning and skipping, and inter-row traversal. Recent learning-based approaches have enabled robust in-row navigation from onboard perception, but navigation across rows typically requires a priori knowledge of field geometry to specify and tune row-transition maneuvers, preventing arbitrary transitions between rows. We address this challenge by framing navigation in these environments as a goal-directed navigation task, where a long-horizon goal is expressed relative to the robot and a planner generates local paths based on the goal and the robot's perceptual observations. We present FlowRow, a flow-matching-based local planner which models the distribution of diverse agricultural navigation behaviors as $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ paths using the long-horizon goal and depth perception. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce RowNavBench, a navigation benchmark for semi-structured agricultural environments developed in Isaac Sim, comprising 900 episodes across grape vineyards, lemon orchards, and apple orchards with varying row lengths, row and plant spacings, plant positions, and weed growth. FlowRow achieves 87% success, compared to 44% for the strongest generative behavior cloning baseline retrained on the same demonstrations. We will release our benchmark, data, and code upon acceptance.

Industry News: Asymmetric Discourse Homogenization on Reddit Was a Text-Length Artifact: A Reanalysis

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (180 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2608.13674v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the first version of this paper I reported that conservative Reddit users began writing more alike after ChatGPT was released while progressive users did not. That result came from a similarity measure that rises and falls with comment length. I redo every analysis of the original paper on all 6,056,593 comments with a sentence encoder and a dispersion measure computed within length strata, and the conservative break goes away. The two camps show no reliable difference in how within-group similarity changed after late 2022, and the ChatGPT date behaves like any of the more than two thousand other cutoffs I test. The matched flair comparison, the cumulative AI index, the stayer panel and the entropy signature each lose their support once length is held fixed. The one change that survives is older. Left and right comments drew closer to each other between 2019 and 2022, and that convergence was complete before ChatGPT arrived. I end with what this implies for studies that measure homogenization with embeddings.

Industry News: The 4 Best Planners of 2027: Roterunner, Hobonichi, Cloth & Paper

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-new planner, and I've found the best planners if you're shopping for something new for 2027. Whether you're looking to get a little more organized or just love having somewhere to write everything down, the beginning of the year is a great time for a fresh start, and most planner companies have their 2027 planner designs already available.

Sources indicate that the world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand. But there's a wide world of options out there that can perfectly suit your needs, especially if you're willing to build your own travel notebook or write in the dates on an undated paper planner, or open to trying your first Japanese-style planner.

Sources indicate that after years of testing and a constant stack of planners on my desk, I've found these standout favorite planner styles that could benefit everyone. If you're looking for a tech companion to your paper planner, check out my guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars and Best Digital Notebooks to help keep your calendar and thoughts organized digitally.

Sources indicate that updated November 2026: I've updated the information in this guide to reflect planner availability as 2026 comes to an end and 2027 designs become available. I'm also currently testing 2027 designs from Plum Paper, Laurel Denise, My PA Planner, and Sterling Ink, plus an undated design of Aura Estelle if you're looking for a planner you can start using in December 2026 into the new year.

According to recent reports, if you need a single planner that can do it all and won't burn through your back-to-school budget, this is the one. The Roterunner Purpose Planner is an undated planner that has monthly spreads, weekly spreads, and two full open pages for each week, so there's plenty of room to write longer lists or a project brainstorm. Each monthly and weekly spread has a ton of premade checklist sections for you to use, too. There's even space to track your meals, water intake, and gratitude. It's a planner that actually helps me stay organized and gives me space to track and take notes without running out of room.

The undated nature makes it easy to pick up anytime and use for whichever months you need. Fell off the boat for a few months? No problem. No pages will go to waste when you can fill them in as you go. It only covers six months, but I actually like that; it once again feels like a feasible commitment, especially if you're waffling on how much paper planner you want to promise to use. I love the massive B5 size ($35) since it's finally enough space for me and all my various to-do lists and brainstorms, but there's also a smaller (and cheaper!) A5 ($28) size. It's truly my go-to planner since it has so much space for me to both use the pre-made lists and the open space to actually stay organized and put all my ideas, intends, and notes into one planner. Most others make me feel like I need a companion notebook, but not the Roterunner.

Recent findings suggest that the covers come in a variety of simple colors, and in both hard cover or soft, but the butter-soft faux leather soft cover is my favorite of the bunch. Get it in B5 size if you're always looking for more room in your journals and planners—you won't regret it.

Amazon (Techo, January 2027 Start).

Amazon (Cousin, January 2027 Start).

Sources indicate that if you're getting into planners, there's no way you won't hear about Hobonichi at some point. There are a few different planners the brand makes, with the Techo being the most popular model. I tested the similar Hobonichi Cousin, which adds weekly spreads to the front of the planner after the monthly overviews. While I don't typically prefer a daily planner style, I was surprised by how much I liked using the Hobonichi. All of Hobonichi's planners use Tomoe River S paper, which is super thin but won't bleed through to the other side. It's also super smooth to the touch and to write on. I liked adding my own structure to the daily pages; I sketched a box to separate my to-do lists and habit trackers from my hourly agenda for the day, and then would usually freeform the rest of the page based on what was on my mind. The Cousin I tested and photographed is an A5 size, while the standard Techo is the smaller A6.

Hobonichi's 2027 editions are here, so you can stock up on your planner for next year right now, plus tons of colors, covers, and other accessories, some of which are unique to 2027. I recommend picking out a protective cover since I did ding up my soft cover quite a bit, and that was just from being used around the house with an occasional trip in a bag. There are little quotes in the corners, but I got a Japanese version instead of an English one, so I can't actually read mine. But honestly, I'm glad I did; I prefer the Japanese lettering to English words on the corners of each page.

Shop (Single Notebook, A5 Slim).

Shop (Clear Vinyl Cover, A5 Slim).

Shop (Travel Notebook Set, A5 Alim).

Industry observers note that I've been obsessed with travel notebooks this year. A travel notebook uses bands to connect three or four notebooks together, and I love using this system to build a customized planner designed for my exact needs. It makes it easy to change the design, too, since you can just switch out a single notebook when it's full.

I really like Cloth & Paper's Travel Notebook Collection. There are 13 different notebooks you can choose from to include in your travel notebook, ranging from classic weekly and monthly spreads to more unique options like a daily wellness notebook and a task planner. It's really a great option if you want a couple of specific things, or even just a regular monthly and weekly notebook plus a blank notebook in the back you can fill with to-do lists and replace anytime without needing an entirely newly introduced planner. It's great for students, too, because you can have a notebook dedicated to tracking your assignments and syllabus for the semester. You'll need to create your own, though, as Cloth & Paper doesn't have a dedicated academic notebook for you to select.

I tried both the A5 Slim and the Pocket Plus size, and I really prefer the A5 Slim for a traditional planner experience. The Pocket Plus would be fun to bring on a trip; I wish I'd had it on my latest trip to store little mementos and key things like parking receipts, and could have also written out notes and the strategy for the week-long trip. But otherwise, the larger A5 slim was much easier to write on and use for my daily notes and planning.

You'll want the Clear Vinyl Travel Notebook Cover ($23 to $25) no matter which size you choose, which includes elastic bindings to bring all the notebooks you buy together, and you can also pick up more colorful elastic options to add a little more personality to your planner.

Erin Condren (Academic Planner).

I've heard a lot of good things about Erin Condren. Founded in 2005 by Erin Condren, it's known for the LifePlanner that's full of various spreads and productivity tools that you can customize, but there are other variations of planners you can find from the brand. While you'll usually customize your Erin Condren planner if you shop directly on the site, there's a predesigned Target line you can shop that won't give you options, but will give you a well-made planner that's ready to go immediately.

It has been revealed that I've been testing the Erin Condren Academic Planner you'll find at Target, but it's sold out as we head into the newly introduced year; Erin Condren's website has similar, but more expensive options with more cover and customization options. This base version from Target is a great fit for students and people with deadline-style or client-based work they want to organize. Each month has two pages following the monthly spread to set your most notable to-dos and dates, but also a full page to track the month's deadlines and what class (or client, or in my case, story beat) they're for. After that, there are weekly spreads with long columns for each day, and seven blocks of four lines that you can label with things like specific classes, clubs, or organizations, or parenting and household tasks, as I track. It's been a really easy planner to add into my lifestyle, even though it's made for students. There's a class tracker in the front of the planner, too, which I skipped using, plus a detailed holiday calendar, and the back has project and exam pages, plus blank note pages, and even a simple sheet of stickers with things like “Exam,” “Midterm,” and “Paper Due.”.

Academic planners usually start in August, so you probably don't want a planner like this if you want something fresh for the latest year. But it's still my favorite I've tried if it's your preferred style. Erin Condren does have annual layouts and its popular LifePlanner designs available in 2027 layouts, and other specific designs like budget planners and teacher lesson planners if you're looking for something specific, too.

Sources indicate that like I remarked, there's a huge world of planners out there. Here are a few that the Reviews team and I at WIRED have tested and enjoyed.

The Kokuyo Jibun Techo is another Japanese planner, but this one is a travel-notebook-style design, making it more customizable with a cover and multiple books that fit inside it. The First Kit comes with three books that fit into the included cover: Diary (labeled simply with the year), Life, and Idea. The 2026 versions are sold out, but you can buy the 2027 versions right now.

Looking for more of a monthly planner? The Big A## Planner is a massive planner with a nice monthly spread you can literally spread across your desk, with plenty of writing space for each day. Best for working from home, though; you don't want to have to fit this into your work bag.

In a recent development, if you're looking for a great daily planner, the Day Designer is a popular option for a reason. It's bulky since it has pages for every single day, but it leaves room for both your schedule and a long to-do list.

Plum Paper (A5 Vertical Priorities).

Plum Paper is my favorite classic-style planner, and you can easily customize it to start at any time of year and design the pages to fit your needs. I especially like the weekly A5 Vertical Priorities layout, and you can add all kinds of customizations into the daily columns, the habit tracker, and more to make it exactly what you want. But I've also left the habit tracker blank so I can adjust my habits as needed all year long.

Sources indicate that I bought this no-frills hardback during Prime Day last year, figuring I couldn’t go wrong for less than 20 bucks, and I was right. It’s a handy A5 size with a monthly view calendar at the beginning of each month, and then a 5-by-2.5-inch square for each day. That’s it. There are some plain lined pages in the back if you need more space for notes, but if your planning consists only of to-do lists and tracking deadlines, you will love this.—Kat Merck.

Recent findings suggest that agendio Basic Planner starting at $48: This is a completely customizable planner. I liked it, and you have the option to design your own pages, and the folder-style cover will protect both the pages and binding. I didn't love the customization tools or abilities as much as I wanted to, and there are a lot of steps to create your planner. I preferred the custom tools of Plum Paper over it. It's a good planner if the pages and binder-style are what you're looking for, and you can find some preset options that usually start around $48 for the smallest page size and black-and-white print.

It has been revealed that ban.do 12-Month Planner for $20: If you're looking for another affordable option but want something with more personality than the Roterunner above, Ban.do's planners are fun and colorful and even come with a page of stickers. It's only a horizontal weekly format, though, which I don't love (but maybe you do!) and the 2027 12-Month designs are now available.

Happy Planner 12-Month Planner for $33: Happy Planner uses disc-bound planners to make it easy to remove and add pages or covers, which is nice for customizability. But they're a very specific aesthetic, and personally, I didn't love turning pages on the discs. Still, it's a good planner if you like the style, and they come in a ton of different layouts. Right now, you can get a Happy Planner that starts in July 2026 and will run you until June 2027, perfect for tracking the academic year.

Laurel Denise Nancy Academic Planner for $44: These planners are cool because you'll look at the month and your weekly at the same time, as the slim weekly pages lay on top of the monthly spread. However, I write way, way too much for the space in these planners, at least for the Nancy design I tested previously. It's great if you just want to write a couple to-dos and meetings per day, but if you want space for detailed lists, you might feel the way I did. I'm currently testing the 2027 Luna ($62) and Scout ($62) planners from Laurel Denise to see if I still feel the same way compared to the original design.

Industry observers note that leuchtturm1917 12-Month Ruled Planner for $29: This is a solid, minimalist planner that has a popular following. It's a simple horizontal weekly layout with the week on one side and a lined page on the other. It's not enough space for everything I write down, but if you're looking for something simple and space for a couple of lists or notes for each week that fit onto a page, it's a good option for you. Leuchtturm1917 also has a nice line of notebooks that look the same from the outside cover, so make sure you actually get the planner.

Muji Undated Weekly Planner for $7: If you want a super simple, super affordable planner, the Muji Undated Weekly is for you. It's just undated weekly horizontal spreads from front to back, even on the paper cover. It's slim, but still more than a year's worth of weeks in it. It's the most minimalist planner I've tried, and though I'm not a fan of horizontal weekly spreads for my planner needs, it's a great cheap option for a lot of people.

According to recent reports, papier Hardcover 2027 Planner for $40: My favorite thing about Papier's planners is how gorgeous the covers are. Papier has a range of beautiful designs you can choose that feel like they belong on a bookshelf rather than just my planner. I tested one of the annual planners, which has the horizontal weekly layout I don't love on any planner (and you can still get that by choosing the mid-year layout for any cover Papier has if you love that style), but the academic one ($29) has a vertical layout that's much more up my alley. Whichever style you like, you can pick. Papier also has softcover academic planners ($32) that use a ring binding, which is easier to lay open than the hard cover binding, and still has both mid-year and academic layout options.

Passion Planner 2027 Planner for $50: This planner was really popular when I was in college, and maybe it still is with the college kids. I liked it, but I feel like the Purpose Planner does a similar thing but better, at least for my needs. It's got vertical spread, but every slot is timed, so I can't use it as a to-do list. It's great for anyone needing to plan out a super detailed schedule and has some to-do list spaces on the bottom, but they're pretty small in my opinion to work for an entire week. It's good for students who only want to track their busy schedules and a couple assignments and tasks for each week.

In a recent development, looking for what to pair with your planner? Here are some of our team's favorite daily tools and planner accessories.

Passion Planner Passion Highlighters for $20: If your planner could use a little color, I really like Passion Planner's highlighter sets. They're nice and thin-tipped to fit into slim planner lines, and I especially like the vintage colors for adding color without it feeling neon-bright. You can use the highlighters to organize your plans by type (I like to do red for work, blue for my kid, yellow for things like doctor's appointments, and green for my social life) or color-code your class subjects like we used to do with ringed notebooks.

Pilot Metropolitan Fountain Pen for $34: I never understood the appeal of a fountain pen until I bought one. A properly smoothed fountain pen nib requires very little pressure to write with and seems to glide across the page with a soft, satisfying scratching sound. I know, I'm one of those people now. Much of my initial skepticism came from the perceived complexity of caring for and using a fountain pen, which is very much overblown. My favorite pen of the dozen I've tested is the Pilot Metropolitan with the fine nib. It's easy to work with, taking either prefilled ink cartridges, which you can pop in and out without ever spilling any ink, or you can fill it yourself using a converter and the ink of your choice. I started off using the cartridges, but eventually my quest for a waterproof ink led me to the converter and this sketching ink. Once a week or so, I dip the Metropolitan nib in the bottle of ink and twist the converter to fill the chamber with ink—that's all there is to it. Whichever fountain pen you find works best for you, you’ll find you'll have a quite simply better writing experience. —Scott Gilbertson.

Plum Paper Seasonal Stickers for $10: There are a lot of stickers out there you could use for your planners, but my favorites—especially for the holidays—are from Plum Paper. They're beautiful and fun, and are mostly nice and small to fit into small lines or monthly charts without eating up the entire section. I like that there's a mix of shapes and styles, and you can also shop stickers for themes like home, fitness, wellness, and baby milestones. You can even make your own custom stickers (starting at $12), which are only thick line-style stickers where you can customize the word and icon on them. Still, very handy!

Not everyone needs or wants a rigid planner. If you just need daily to-do lists or are a fan of bullet journals, consider getting a great notebook instead.

Maybe you just want a plain, lined notebook. One of our former reviewers recommended the Midori MD Notebook, and I found it to be a nice small size if you're looking for something minimal. It comes in lined, unlined, or dot-grid, and uses paper made from cotton pulp (just like money!) Midori’s notebooks are designed to fit inside notebook or journal covers (which you can find all over Etsy). The pages are a subtle off-white and have a weight and texture that draw you in.

According to recent reports, one of our reviewers skips a planner entirely and instead writes down his to-do list on a 3-by-5 index card. He puts that index card into his pocket with a pocket-sized memo book like this one from Field Notes ($13 for three), where he jots down notes throughout the day to use for the next day's to-do list. Both the notebook and index cards fit inside a waxed canvas notebook cover to keep them safe from the elements (or just his pocket). It's an affordable and easy-to-manage system.

Industry observers note that studies show that it's good for your brain to write things down. Sure, you could put your calendar in an online tool, but putting pen to paper activates more brain connectivity. We're more likely to remember and learn things if we write them down by hand, so using a paper planner for your to-do list can make it easier to remember. Plus, it's fun! You're given a creative space to let out everything you need to remember, from appointments to the day's tasks, and customize it in a way that best helps you stay organized.

What Style Paper Planner Is Best for You?

Industry observers note that paper planners mainly come in two styles: weekly and daily. Daily planners have an entire page dedicated to each day, while weekly planners have an entire week spread across just two pages. These aren't the only options (monthly is another popular one, for example, but not as popular as these two styles), but they're the most common you'll see. I like daily planners for folks who have a really busy schedule they want to initiative out, and long daily to-do lists. Weekly planners are great if you want to be able to write down a few things per day but don't need an entire page.

What Sizes Do Planners Come In?

Here are a couple common planner sizes. My favorite are the larger sizes since I like lots of room to doodle, but the smaller A5 is a popular choice for a book-sized planner that won't take up too much space. Not all paper planners use the same sizing names—Moleskine, for example, calls its A5 size a large—so you'll want to check measurements before you purchase.

In a recent development, arXiv:2509.20591v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is an efficient numerical algorithm for computation of long-ranged forces in $N$-body problems within gravitational and electrostatic fields. This method utilizes multipole expansions of the Green's function inherent to the underlying dynamical systems. Despite its widespread application in physics and engineering, the integration of FMM with modern machine learning architectures remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a novel neural network architecture, the Neural FMM, that integrates the information flow of the FMM into a hierarchical machine learning framework for learning the Green's operator of an Elliptic PDE. Our Neural FMM architecture leverages a hierarchical computation flow of the FMM method to split up the local and far-field interactions and efficiently learn their respective representations.

This concept paper defines the framework's scope, semantically and statistically, and specifies a protocol for its empirical testing. The population-level claims it is designed to support therefore belong to a staged research program rather than to results claimed here. Measurement standardization underpins three claims. The first is a reliability claim: under bounded conditions, large language models can produce reliable, standardized assessments of the evidential and policy alignment of expert-AI interactions. The second is a governance claim: alignment scores give experts an immediate signal during deployment and give institutions a basis for monitoring alignment patterns across mission types, models, and domains. The third is an outcome validation claim: once measurement standardization is established, aggregate alignment scores could be used to study associations with downstream outcomes in regulated professional settings. This introduces the possibility of an "AI epidemiology", a form of risk detection based on correlated variables instead of mechanistic analysis, inspired by epidemiological reasoning. A minimal application of the protocol to a published expert-AI corpus shows that the judge reproduces its policy and evidential alignment scores across two runs under the specified conditions. Judge reliability at scale remains to be validated in future work. The paper sets out a defined grammar of eight interaction fields, together with a statistical protocol based on paired bootstrap inference, DeLong's test for paired AUCs as a sensitivity check, a pre-specified one-sided non-inferiority margin of 0.05, and Holm-Bonferroni correction.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22289v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Panels in economics, finance and climate science are often driven by common components that differ in memory, such as common trends, cycles, or joint shocks. We study approximate factor models whose common factors are fractionally integrated with heterogeneous and unknown memory and develop the asymptotic theory of principal components for the panel in levels. Our theory builds on the eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix being ordered by memory asymptotically: a nonstationary factor group with memory $d>1/2$ generates eigenvalues of order $NT^{2d-1}$, whereas stationary factors generate eigenvalues of order $N$. Principal components estimate the factors consistently up to rotation, while adjacent factor groups are separated at a rate given by their memory gap. The information criteria of Bai and Ng remain consistent for the total number of factors, with their penalties acting as thresholds on eigenvalues that are asymptotically ordered by factor memory. When the nonstationary factors lose their variance advantage, estimation in levels remains consistent, whereas after differencing the factors can become undetectable. A Monte Carlo study shows that factor-number selection in levels tolerates more idiosyncratic noise than selection after first differencing. For monthly temperatures at $308$ European weather stations, our methods select two factors. The first is a persistent common warming factor. The estimated common component implies that 2021-2025 was $2.15^\circ\mathrm{C}$ warmer than 1960-1990, with the strongest warming in Eastern Europe. After first differencing, the criterion selects one factor, and loses regional heterogeneity as compared to the model in levels.

Map-free prediction improves deployment flexibility by removing the dependence on high-definition maps, but it also loses explicit road-topology and lane-connectivity priors. Consequently, the model must recover stable motion cues from short histories while resolving prospective interaction relations without lane-level guidance. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a map-free trajectory prediction framework centered on a novel Goal-Conditioned Expert-Routed Transformer (GCERT). A lightweight intra-agent front-end first decomposes projected historical motion features into a smooth trend and a local detail residual through a centered moving average. Component-specific residual projections transform the two signals before a causal temporal Transformer summarizes their recombined evolution. GCERT employs dual-level expert routing: edge-level relation experts generate interaction-specific messages, while node-level state experts adapt the transformation after message aggregation. Predicted motion goals update the node representations and construct prospective relative-geometry and orientation edge features before the final interaction layer, thereby conditioning attention, relation-specific message generation, and state transformation. GCERT therefore determines not only which neighboring agents should be attended to, but also what relation-specific information should be transmitted and how the aggregated node state should be transformed. The resulting representations are decoded into multimodal future trajectories and jointly optimized with trajectory-regression, mode-classification, and goal-prediction objectives.

Industry News: DiScoFormer: One transformer for density and score, across distributions

📅 29 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, many problems in machine learning and the sciences come down to the same task: you have a collection of data points and want to recover the distribution they came from—which values are common, and which are rare.
  • Sources indicate that diffusion-based generative models (the technology behind AI image generators like Stable Diffusion and DALL-E) start from random noise and repeatedly follow the score, turning that noise into a realistic image.
  • Recent findings suggest that extracting the density and score from a finite sample is challenging, and today's tools force a trade-off between generalizability and accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech report: arxiv.org/abs/2511.05924.

According to recent reports, many problems in machine learning and the sciences come down to the same task: you have a collection of data points and want to recover the distribution they came from—which values are common, and which are rare. Pinning down that distribution means estimating two quantities: the distribution's density and, more useful as dimensionality grows, its score. The density is the smooth version of a histogram—high where points cluster and low where they're scarce. The score—the gradient of the log-density—points in the direction the density rises fastest: move a point along the score and it heads toward a more probable region.

Sources indicate that diffusion-based generative models (the technology behind AI image generators like Stable Diffusion and DALL-E) start from random noise and repeatedly follow the score, turning that noise into a realistic image. The same score drives Bayesian sampling and the particle simulations used to model systems such as plasma.

Recent findings suggest that extracting the density and score from a finite sample is challenging, and today's tools force a trade-off between generalizability and accuracy. One classical approach, kernel density estimation (KDE), computes the density at any location from the data points around it: the closer and more numerous they are, the higher the density. It needs no training and applies to any distribution, but its accuracy falls off sharply as dimensionality grows. Alternatively, neural score-matching models trained to predict the score stay accurate even in high dimensions, but each needs to learn the distribution and must be retrained from scratch for another.

We introduce a upcoming solution called the DiScoFormer (Density and Score Transformer)—one model that, given a set of data points, estimates both the density and the score of the distribution in a single forward pass without retraining.

DiScoFormer maps an entire sample to the density and score of the distribution behind it using stacked layers of transformer blocks. The model utilizes cross-attention, which allows it to evaluate density and score at any point—not just where you have data. Score and density share a mathematical relationship: score is the gradient of the logarithm of density. We leverage this by having a shared backbone with two output heads, one for the density and one for the score.

According to recent reports, this coupling does more than save parameters. The score head has to match the gradient of the log-density head at every query, so any gap between them is a label-free consistency loss. We use this at inference—hold the context fixed, take a few gradient steps on that consistency loss, and DiScoFormer adapts itself to an out-of-distribution input on the spot, no ground-truth density or score required.

There's a mathematical reason why the transformer architecture fits this task. Kernel density estimation has a single bandwidth—how far each point's influence reaches, fixed in advance and applied identically everywhere. Attention is a strict generalization of it: we analytically show that a single attention head's weights are nearly a Gaussian kernel over the data, so one cross-attention block can already reproduce KDE's density and score. From there the model goes further, learning several such scales at once and adapting them to the data. DiScoFormer doesn't discard the classical method for a black box but instead includes KDE as a special case and improves on it.

What data did we use to train DiScoFormer? We relied on Gaussian Mixture Models for two primary reasons. Firstly, GMMs are universal density approximators—with enough components they match essentially any smooth distribution to arbitrarily small error. Secondly, GMMs have closed-form densities and scores, so we always have an exact target to supervise against. We employ both of these properties by drawing a upcoming GMM for every batch, giving the model virtually unlimited examples of target distributions and supervising each against a given GMM's exact density and score.

According to recent reports, across the board, DiScoFormer beats KDE at both density and score estimation, and the gap widens exactly where KDE struggles. In 100 dimensions, it isn't close—against the best hand-tuned KDE, it cuts score error by about 6.5x and density error by more than 37x, and it keeps improving as you add samples, while KDE runs out of memory. It also travels far outside its training data, staying accurate on mixtures with more modes than it ever saw during training and on non-Gaussian shapes like the Laplace and Student-t. KDE's main advantage remains speed, especially when datasets are small.

The part about DiScoFormer that we find most promising is that score estimation is a shared dependency across many fields, such as generative modeling, Bayesian inference, and scientific computing. A pretrained, plug-in estimator that stays accurate in high dimensions and removes the need to retrain per problem could cut that cost across all of them at once—one model, reused everywhere score and density show up.

We encourage you to read our technical report for more details.

The limitation is both physical and algorithmic. A compact head leaves little room for densely packed, independently controllable actuation; meanwhile, learned systems often generate an avatar video, landmarks, or facial parameters and then infer actuator commands through visual retargeting. By decoupling actuator placement from facial action points, it enables coordinated full-face expression within a compact volume. On the algorithmic side, ROSE-VAE learns an identity-independent shared facial-motion latent space from human, digital-human, and robot observations. ROSE-Flow directly maps text, audio, or their combination to trajectories in this motion space without using video as a generator input. ROSE-ACT then converts these trajectories into constrained actuator commands. Our system demonstrates how high-density biomimetic hardware and a shared executable facial-motion representation can jointly unify cross-embodiment learning, multimodal generation, and physical robot expression.

arXiv:2607.24651v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reliable visual document understanding requires a model to attribute each answer to the evidence regions that support it. Recent benchmarks and systems express this step through a coordinate interface: the model outputs the coordinates of bounding boxes that mark the evidence regions in the document. Under this interface, vision-language models often fail to identify the right regions even when the answer is correct, a failure known as Attribution Hallucination. We present a study that investigates whether this failure is partially limited by what the model can express through coordinates. On a verified bilingual CiteVQA subset, we compare the coordinate interface with a language interface in which the model outputs only text, quoting its evidence verbatim, and a multimodal retriever returns the location of each quote as a page region proposed by a layout parser (tables and figures are quoted through their captions or notes); the comparison is repeated over six open vision-language models. Compared with the coordinate interface, evidence recall rises from at most 8 points to between 26 and 47 and the hallucination rate roughly halves, with little change in answer quality. Building on this comparison, we use the same quote-and-retrieve pipeline as a training scaffold: because region-level evidence labels are expensive to collect for long documents, we introduce a GRPO recipe whose reward is a judge's reading of the gold answer and crops of the retrieved regions, training the model to quote better evidence without any region labels and raising an 8B backbone's strict attributed accuracy from 22.4 to 33.8. These findings indicate a practical path to improve attribution without a coordinate interface and without costly region-level supervision.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2508.20262v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate intermediate reasoning steps before producing answers, improving performance on challenging problems by iteratively developing solutions. There is evidence that LRMs expend more effort on the problems that take people longer to solve, but it is unclear whether these relationships hold on more subjective tasks without verifiable answers. This study addresses this problem through an experiment using a content moderation task, where task difficulty is manipulated by varying the relative offensiveness of two different options. Comparing six large reasoning models with 1,854 human subjects, we find that models expend more reasoning effort, measured using the length of the chain-of-thought (CoT), on the kinds of cases that take people longer to adjudicate. People took 31\% longer and models produced 51 to 306\% longer CoTs when offensiveness was held constant across the two posts. The correlation is relatively low for individual decisions ($r = 0.15$--$0.19$), but average response times and average reasoning effort are closely correlated when tasks are grouped by the types of offensive language ($r = 0.85$--$0.93$). Qualitative analyses of the CoT summaries from Gemini 2.5 Pro corroborate these findings, showing that secondary factors were mentioned more often when offensiveness was fixed. The results point to the potential for using reasoning traces to prioritize difficult cases and enhance interpretability.

Tech Report: Featuring Every Eval Ever Results on Hugging Face Model Pages

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that every Eval Ever (EEE) and Hugging Face Community Evals are now intercompatible.
  • EEE rolled out in February 2026 as a project of the EvalEval Coalition, the first cross-institutional effort to improve how AI evaluation results get reported by both first and third party evaluators.
  • Evaluation results are how we measure model capabilities, compare models against each other, and reason about safety and governance, and yet they are scattered and hard to compare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that every Eval Ever (EEE) and Hugging Face Community Evals are now intercompatible. We enable cross-posting and interpreting evaluation results, while linking to open models, leaderboards, and a unified standardized metadata store.

EEE rolled out in February 2026 as a project of the EvalEval Coalition, the first cross-institutional effort to improve how AI evaluation results get reported by both first and third party evaluators. Hugging Face launched Community Evals in February 2026 to decentralize how benchmark scores get reported on the Hub. Combined, they patch gaps in how consumers, researchers, and policymakers trust, understand, and choose evaluations and models.

Evaluation results are how we measure model capabilities, compare models against each other, and reason about safety and governance, and yet they are scattered and hard to compare. They live in papers, leaderboards, blog posts, and harness logs, among others, each in its own format. The same model on the same benchmark often returns different scores depending on who ran it and how; LLaMA 65B, for one, has been reported at both 63.7 and 48.8 on MMLU. These gaps can arise from evaluation settings that we found are commonly unreported.

EEE is our fix for the reporting side. It's one JSON schema for an evaluation result that records:.

The schema was built with feedback from researchers and policy researchers, and it takes in results from any source, so harness logs, leaderboard scrapes, and paper numbers all end up in the same shape. The GitHub repository has the converters, examples, and a contributor guide. Since launching, the datastore on Hugging Face has grown to around 229,000 evaluation results across more than 22,000 models and 2,200 benchmarks, pulled from 31 different reporting formats. Reproducing just those runs from scratch would cost somewhere in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, which is a reasonable argument for not letting the data scatter once someone has paid to generate it.

Learn more about the schema and how to contribute here.

Now, it comes with better integration and attribution. Contributors can now send EEE results to Hugging Face Community Evals. We built a converter that takes your EEE records and writes the small YAML files Hugging Face expects, so you don't have to keep the same result in two formats by hand.

This is newly introduced functionality for everyone who reports or reads evaluations, not only existing EEE contributors. First-party evaluators reporting on their own models and third-party evaluators reporting on someone else's can both submit to Community Evals and to EEE, and anyone browsing the Hub gets results that trace back to a full record. When you submit your data through your organization's official Hugging Face account, your results show up with a verified checkmark on EvalEval, a signal to readers that the numbers come straight from the source. The rest of this post walks through what Community Evals are and what the converter does.

Hugging Face Community Evals has two sides.

According to recent reports, A benchmark lives in a dataset repo that registers itself by adding an eval.yaml. Once registered, that dataset page collects and displays a leaderboard of every score reported against it across the Hub. The list of official benchmarks grows over time.

A model's scores live in .eval_results/*.yaml inside the model repo. They show up on the model card and feed into the matching benchmark leaderboard. Both the model author's own results and results submitted by anyone else through a pull request get aggregated, and each score carries a badge saying whether it was author-submitted, community-submitted, or independently verified. Anyone can add a score to any model by opening a PR with the right YAML file, and the model author can close PRs or hide results on their own repo.

Here is what one of these leaderboards looks like:.

Community Evals Leaderboard for Humanity's Last Exam on the Hub.

Industry observers note that this is where EEE and Community Evals fit together. When you send a result to both, two things happen: First, your score appears on the Hugging Face model page and gets pulled into the benchmark's leaderboard. And second, it carries a source badge that links straight back to the full EEE record, where the generation config, the harness version, the reproducibility notes, and any instance-level data live.

An Evaluation (MMLU-Pro) from EEE Datastore (a) cross-linked at the file level to a Hugging Face model card (b). The Source EvalEval badge links to the full JSON record.

The two destinations do different jobs toward the same goal. Hugging Face puts your result where people look at models, with a link back to the source. EEE keeps the full structured record that makes the result interpretable, and powers Eval Cards on top of it. Send your data to both and the same evaluation ends up visible and legible at once, which is the point of reporting one at all.

Sources indicate that you can see that cross-compatibility below. The same GPQA scores that surface on the model card above also render in Eval Cards, which composes the EEE run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record. Same evaluation, a different surface:.

Hugging Face stores eval scores in the model repo as a YAML under .eval_results/. The required fields are just the benchmark dataset, the task, and the value. The source block is the part that creates the backlink to EEE.

Sources indicate that the converter fills this in from your existing records. It maps source_data.hf_repo to dataset.id, evaluation_name to task_id, score_details.score to value, and evaluation_timestamp to date, then drops in the datastore object URL as the source link to the per-record EEE JSON. It currently handles four of the official benchmarks: MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE, and GSM8K.

In a recent development, the converter does more than reshape fields. You point it at one EEE datastore collection and it downloads that collection along with the records it references, checks the object hashes, and finds the scores that map to a supported benchmark. Before it writes anything live it audits what already exists: it reads every .eval_results YAML on the model's main branch and in open PRs, and compares by dataset and task rather than by filename. If a score is already there it is marked already_present, if a different score is there it is flagged as a score_conflict, and if the model repo doesn't resolve on the Hub it is marked missing_hf_model. Everything else is marked ready.

According to recent reports, nothing gets pushed without your sign-off. The tool writes local YAML previews and a review file you can inspect, shows a report of what is ready and what needs attention, and only opens PRs after you type OPEN PRS and enter a commit message. Reruns reuse the cached results for a collection unless you pass --force.

The converter's review step. Excluded entries (here, models with no matching Hub repo) are listed with their EEE source URLs, and the ready PRs wait on an explicit OPEN PRS confirmation.

Submit your full records to the EEE datastore.

Utilizing EEE requires only one additional step, which the converter largely automates. The community eval converter tool can be found in the GitHub repository. To process a collection, execute the following:.

In a recent development, review the previews and the report it generates, then type OPEN PRS when you're ready to submit. Full documentation for the schema, CLI, and converters is at evalevalai.com/every_eval_ever/hf-community-evals.

In response to this, Topological Deep Learning (TDL) leverages more general combinatorial representations--such as simplicial or cellular complexes--to accommodate higher-order interactions. Existing TDL methods often extend GNNs through Higher-Order Message Passing (HOMP), but face critical scalability challenges due to the steep complexity overhead of propagating messages through combinatorial structures. To overcome this limitation, we propose HOPSE (Higher-Order Positional and Structural Encoder), a framework free of learnable message passing layers that uses Hasse graph decompositions to derive efficient and expressive encodings over arbitrary higher-order domains. Notably, HOPSE training and inference scale linearly with the size of combinatorial representations while preserving the expressive power and permutation equivariance of the HOMP approaches. Experiments on molecular and topological benchmarks show that it matches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance while consistently achieving speedups over HOMP-based models, opening a new path for scalable TDL. Sources indicate that arXiv:2607.07646v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Does RL post-training merely amplify primitive skills already latent in a base model, or can it compose primitive skills into new higher-level strategies? We study this question in a fully observable rewrite-grammar environment where the pretraining distribution is known and every generated rewrite can be audited. A Transformer is pretrained on primitive symbol-rewrite chains and post-trained on a Trace-based reasoning task with only a binary final-answer reward. RL solves held-out problems that remain rarely solved by the pretrained model even under much larger sampling budgets, while rejection fine-tuning improves early but plateaus. Trace analysis shows that RL reorganizes primitive competence through a phased compositional mechanism: it first strengthens primitive reductions, then discovers valid composed procedures. These include sequential compositions, which collapse ordered chains of primitive contractions, and parallel compositions, which combine independent primitive contractions in a single step. The composed procedures are not isolated samples; they are reused and consolidated into a stable repertoire. Comparing RL with rejection fine-tuning shows that the key difference is not exploration volume but selectivity: RFT produces many shortcut-like rewrites, much of them invalid, whereas RL concentrates exploration into valid reusable structure. Pretraining ablations show that the emergence of compositional strategies is gated not by primitive exposure alone, but by whether pretraining organizes primitive competence into reduction procedures that RL can later compress. The base model provides weak procedural ingredients; RL builds them into reliable higher-level strategies.

Neural CBFs can learn more informative barriers from data, yet a learned barrier is usually verified only for one fixed obstacle configuration. We study whether one neural barrier can be reused across environments by expressing the state relative to each obstacle. The key gap is that these relative coordinates may discard information needed to predict their own evolution. We give a generalized closure condition that represents this missing information as a residual and a lifting theorem that transfers a verified relative-coordinate barrier to every obstacle in a family. A rank test also identifies when symmetry alone cannot justify the transfer. We validate the conditions on a double integrator, a planar aircraft, and a 12-state quadrotor. Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2503.00547v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In graph-level learning, graph neural networks are typically applied with a fixed computational template: the same depth, local message-passing operator, and global attention mechanism are used for every input graph. However, different graphs within the same dataset can vary substantially in prediction difficulty and may require different mixtures of local and non-local computation. We study this phenomenon as graph-level heterogeneity in both classification and regression tasks. To address it, we propose SiGMA (Sigmoid Gated Message-Passing and Attention), a gated hybrid graph neural network architecture that combines message-passing and attention heads within each layer. Inspired by the growing use of gated attention and gated computation in large language models and vision transformers, each head in SiGMA is modulated by a learned node-wise sigmoid gate, allowing the model to adaptively regulate which local or global mechanisms are active for different nodes, layers, and input graphs. The resulting architecture can emulate expressive message-passing backbones, admits near-identity computation paths that are not forced to over-smooth, and enables direct non-local communication beyond message-passing neighborhoods to mitigate over-squashing. Empirically, SiGMA achieves strong performance across graph-level benchmarks, consistently matching or improving over competitive graph transformer and hybrid baselines. Our results suggest that adapting computation to graph-level heterogeneity is a promising direction for building more flexible and effective graph learning architectures.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2607.05114v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA adapt large models through a single low-rank revision. Such updates are susceptible to gradient interference: when a training stream interleaves multiple operational contexts, conflicting updates to shared adapter weights collapse the adapter into an unspecialized average. While recent methods introduce block-wise isolation to remedy this problem, their topologies are static and cannot adapt to context switching or localized sensor degradation. In this work, we introduce Localized LoRA-MoE, a framework that combines localized spatial blocking with context-conditioned expert routing. We propose and evaluate two architectural variants: Block-Wise LoRA-MoE (centralized routing), which modulates the entire structural grid through a single context-conditioned gate, and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE (decentralized routing), which assigns an independent gate to every coordinate cell of the matrix grid. Across three structured transformation benchmarks--a high-dimensional SVD matrix simulation, context-switched transformations over real tabular data, and spatial reconstruction under simulated sensor occlusion--both variants outperform static baselines under comparable adapter budgets. Both variants perform similarly when context shifts the grid uniformly, while cell-wise routing is strictly better when contexts are spatially heterogeneous. When fine-tuning a language model on six interleaved GLUE tasks, task-conditioned routing at a fixed adapter budget outperforms LoRA and static localized adapters, matching per-task adapters with 6x budgets. At decoder scale on Qwen2.5-1.5B, both routed variants outperform static baselines across eight commonsense benchmarks, with cell-wise routing achieving +3.9 points over LoRA at matched active capacity.
