💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang.
  • But just as he’s leaving, the tech giant has a growing list of competitors with a range of upcoming, advanced technology breathing down its neck.
  • According to recent reports, “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI manufacturer, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.

But just as he’s leaving, the tech giant has a growing list of competitors with a range of upcoming, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.

According to recent reports, “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI manufacturer, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.

Already, competitors have started to move in.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.

Industry observers note that significant US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.

Recent findings suggest that several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.

Industry observers note that patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, indicates the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.

And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead remarked, an area where Nvidia barely competes.

It has been revealed that nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.

In a recent development, in 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The tech giant’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.

While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.

In a recent development, huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.

According to recent reports, huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.

In a recent development, babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.

Industry observers note that even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.

Recent findings suggest that most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.

Moorhead states the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.

But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.

But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.

Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.

Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he notes. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.

Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, states Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the tech giant’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.

“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he claims.

PRX Part 4: Our Data Strategy

📅 06 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parts 1 to 3 covered model architectures, training design, and a 24-hour speedrun.
  • In one sentence: we assemble training data from a mix of public and internal datasets, re-caption the images with a VLM, and turn the result into the streamable corpus we trained PRX on.
  • At a high level, the data pipeline looks like this:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome back! This is Part 4 of the PRX series. Parts 1 to 3 covered model architectures, training design, and a 24-hour speedrun. This time we're pulling back the curtain on the part that quietly underpins all of it: the data. Of all the things that shaped PRX's quality, the data pipeline was one of the least glamorous parts to build but nevertheless an notable piece to get right. Here's what we did, what we'd do differently, and a few things we only learned the slow way.

In one sentence: we assemble training data from a mix of public and internal datasets, re-caption the images with a VLM, and turn the result into the streamable corpus we trained PRX on.

At a high level, the data pipeline looks like this:.

In the following we will dive into it in detail.

The goal was to assemble a large, diverse dataset for pre-training. At this stage the model is learning how the world looks: the visual concepts, the objects and scenes, how things are composed and lit, and the sheer range of what images can contain. That is a problem of coverage and diversity, not of per-image perfection. A broad, representative corpus teaches the model far more about the structure of the visual world than a smaller, prettier one would, even if many of the individual images are ordinary snapshots or slightly compressed. Over-filtering for aesthetics at this stage would actually hurt, narrowing the distribution and costing the model concepts and compositional variety it cannot recover later. Making generations look polished is a separate, later concern, which we leave to fine-tuning and preference alignment on small, ruthlessly curated sets. Pre-training is for breadth; fine-tuning is for taste.

It has been revealed that we assemble our pre-training data from a mix of public and internal datasets. The priority at this stage is breadth, diversity, and standing on curation that already exists rather than redoing it ourselves. Where a source already comes quality-filtered, deduplicated, and filtered for NSFW content and personal information, we build on that work instead of repeating it at scale. Sources arrive in different shapes: some come with the image data itself, others as metadata plus baseline captions that we bring into a common form. We took a pragmatic approach: rather than build a corpus entirely from scratch, we leaned on existing datasets and our own tooling to assemble one swiftly. In hindsight it is not necessarily the absolute best dataset one could build, but it was a solid and lightweight starting point for pre-training a 7B model.

In our experience, what matters most for pre-training is to use long captions that accurately describe everything in the image. We saw this directly in Part 2, where switching from short captions to long ones substantially improved sample quality. If captioning is faithful, we don't need to worry about the occasional screenshot, advertisement, logo, or bit of text in an image, because those things get described in the caption too, so the model learns them as conditioned, controllable attributes rather than reproducing them unconditionally. Accurate captioning turns "noise" into something you can prompt for, or prompt away. This is precisely why the filtering we do later is deliberately light. We remove what is genuinely unusable, not everything that is imperfect.

Industry observers note that we have been using Mosaic Streaming and Mosaic Data Shards (MDS) as a dataset format for distributed training for a while now. In combination with Mosaic Composer we found it to be a very low-maintenance, flexible, and well-performing framework for distributed training. Furthermore, MDS datasets can easily and effectively be mixed and shuffled and also allow for distributed training directly from object storage like S3 or GCS.

However, MDS datasets are very rigid. Adding a column or creating a subset for a given filter basically means that one has to scan and rewrite the whole dataset. That's why we use Lance for this kind of feature engineering and dataset curation. Lance is a columnar data format with cheap predicate pushdown, scalar indexes, and vector search, the right tool for building and exploring datasets with billions of rows.

These two formats play off each other throughout this post and the PRX data pipeline: Lance to build, MDS to stream.

Industry observers note that for previous training runs, we used T5Gemma as the text encoder and pre-computed the text latents, storing them in MDS as bytes. This time around, after switching the text encoder to Qwen3-VL, we decided to compute text latents on the fly during training instead. Running the text encoder inside the training loop costs throughput, but how much depends on the model: for a small denoiser it can be significant, whereas at PRX's 7B scale the text encoder's compute is negligible next to the denoiser, and we measured only a roughly 3–4% throughput cost (about 1 extra day on a 30-day run). In return we get two things. Skipping pre-computation keeps our MDS shards much smaller, small enough to store the full pre-training dataset on the SSD-backed shared filesystem of our SLURM cluster rather than streaming it over the network from object storage. And it keeps us free to change the text encoder later without rewriting terabytes of stored latents, which is exactly the kind of switch we made when moving to Qwen3-VL.

We encoded all images as JPEG at quality 92, instead of a lossless format such as PNG. We did not just assume quality 92 was safe, we measured it. Real-world images have usually already been JPEG-compressed several times, so the real question is whether one more re-encode hurts. Across repeated decode/encode cycles on both high-resolution (1–2 MP) and lower-resolution (0.25–0.5 MP) real images, the first re-encode at quality 92 is essentially imperceptible. Each further cycle adds almost nothing, because JPEG promptly converges to a stable state, and even after 10 cycles the images stay well within the imperceptible range, while PNG would be 3–10× larger for no perceptual gain. The numbers, averaged over 100 images at quality 92 and measured against the original (higher PSNR and lower LPIPS are better):.

Since most source images already arrive JPEG-compressed, storing them losslessly as PNG buys little, so we convert everything to JPEG at high quality (quality 92).

Sources indicate that we also checked what matters most: whether training on JPEGs changes what the model produces. Our corpus is mostly JPEG anyway, so the only advantage PNG could offer is not introducing latest artifacts. We deliberately drew the comparison from high-resolution sources, on the expectation that even originally-JPEG images carry few artifacts at high resolution. We trained two identical PRX models at 1024px on the same images, one stored as PNG and one as JPEG at quality 92. Both trained equally well on our metrics, and their generations were practically indistinguishable, including when we estimated how JPEG-compressed the outputs look using a known technique for estimating JPEG quality by matching quantization tables:.

According to recent reports, the detection rate is the fraction of generations in which any quantization structure is found at all. The mean and median estimated JPEG quality are taken over only those flagged images. The two models are practically indistinguishable: only about one generation in ten from either shows any detectable quantization structure, and the differences are small enough that we are confident the training image format has a minimal effect on output quality. So high-quality JPEG storage adds nothing measurable on top of what the sources already carry. For large-scale text-to-image training that is more than good enough. For artifact-sensitive data used to train other Photoroom models, such as our custom AI Shadows model, we still rely on PNGs.

Sources indicate that you cannot interactively explore Parquet tables with hundreds of millions or even billions of rows. We therefore store the data in Lance, where we can index, query, and browse it. We run the ingest with Ray Data, reading the source tables in parallel and writing many fragments of a Lance table across the cluster.

According to recent reports, one lesson worth sharing is about fragmentation. A Lance table is split into fragments, and several operations scale with the total number of fragments rather than the row count: a scan opens the files of every fragment, and some metadata operations are O(number of fragments). A table broken into too many small fragments therefore queries slowly no matter its size. The Lance performance guidance is to keep that count low (the rule of thumb is on the order of a hundred fragments even for a billion-row table) and to run compaction periodically to merge small fragments into larger ones.

We learned this the slow way. Our first ingest targeted only 100,000 rows per fragment, which left thousands of tiny fragments and made even simple filters and full-text queries crawl. After compacting up to roughly a million rows per fragment, which for our tables of several hundred million rows meant on the order of a thousand fragments, queries were fast and we stopped worrying about it. The right target depends on row width, query patterns, and how the data is written, and in hindsight fewer, larger fragments might have been a better default. Lance supports distributed compaction (for example via the Lance-Ray integration), so it is easy to adjust after the fact, but it pays not to over-fragment in the first place.

We chose to re-caption every image ourselves rather than rely on the captions some of the datasets happened to ship with. The reason is consistency: across a mix of sources, caption length, style, and quality vary a lot, and we wanted a single uniform standard across the whole corpus (more on the captioner in Section 3).

The metadata a dataset already carries is still valuable, though, just for a different purpose. Pre-existing captions, and the vector embeddings that sometimes come alongside them (for example CLIP embeddings), are what make a dataset explorable in Lance right away: full-text search over the captions and nearest-neighbor search over an embedding column let us navigate the data and quickly judge its quality and the filtering it will need, well before we have run our own captioning over it. So we keep both, joining them in when they live in a separate table, and lean on them for the browsing we describe next.

Sources indicate that with the data queryable, we could swiftly profile it. The resolution distribution, for example, told us where to set cutoffs. Our smallest training bucket is 512² pixels, and we cap upscaling into a bucket at 4/3 (about 33%), so the effective cutoff is 384² ≈ 147k pixels plus an aspect ratio in [0.5, 2.0]. Everything below that we discard.

Sources indicate that lance tables support full-text search on text columns as well as nearest-neighbor similarity search on vector embedding columns out of the box, and both can be accelerated by building indexes. We did exactly that for the caption and embedding columns, then built a small UI to browse the dataset: real-time text search over the captions as well as navigating clusters of visually similar images via vector search.

Sources indicate that browsing the data this way let us assess its diversity and quality qualitatively and spot issues early, simply by looking at it. We found uninformative baseline captions, a surprising amount of non-photographic content (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics), and some near-duplicate images. These observations shaped the rest of the pipeline directly: re-caption everything (longer, accurate captions describe even imperfect images well, and guarantee that the caption matches the exact image we train on), and add light filtering and deduplication passes later. In general, we believe this sort of exploration tool is invaluable for getting a feel for a dataset before committing to it.

According to recent reports, we found that long, detailed captions are a very strong lever on output quality. In an early benchmark we trained a small diffusion model twice on the same images, once on captions we generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and once on much shorter captions (produced with LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B), and scored both over training. The long captions generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B won across the board, with lower FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD at every checkpoint (lower is better on all three).

Industry observers note that A small diffusion model trained on Qwen2.5-VL-7B captions (red) versus the baseline LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B captions (blue), scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three metrics.

Final metrics (around 100k steps):.

Here is an example image with both our long, VLM-generated caption as well as the shorter caption used as the baseline:.

Our captioning runs as a streaming pipeline built on Ray Data: it reads the data from Lance, prepares each image, captions it on the GPU, and writes the caption back as a newly introduced column we can query and filter on. We prompt for a single dense, visually grounded paragraph rather than a one-line caption.

A tight schedule and limited resources meant that we couldn't spend too much time on ablations of different captioning models and system prompts.

We used the following prompts to generate the captions.

We shortlisted three VLMs as captioner candidates:.

It has been revealed that we benchmarked caption quality indirectly: we trained a small diffusion model for 100k steps on each caption variant and scored its generations with FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD. Alongside the three candidates we scored two reference captioners, to connect this comparison to the first benchmark: the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B (the same model as in the benchmark above) and a set of Gemini 1.5 Flash captions we had generated earlier for the 1M-image internal test set used here. The Gemini captions are a similar length but were produced with a different prompt (all others use the system prompt above), so its curve is indicative rather than a like-for-like comparison.

According to recent reports, FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD over training for the three captioner candidates and two reference captioners, scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three.

Final metrics (around 100k steps):.

Industry observers note that among the candidates, Qwen3.5-9B is best on all three metrics, with Qwen3-VL-8B close behind on FID and DINO-MMD (though weaker on CMMD) and the Relaxed captioner trailing on FID but competitive elsewhere. The clearest result is that the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B — the same model that beat the baseline in the first benchmark — is now the weakest of the five, which is exactly why we didn't just keep it: a caption-tuned or newer model measurably helps. (Gemini 1.5 Flash lands mid-pack, but with the different-prompt caveat above.).

Recent findings suggest that we put less weight on throughput than quality, but at hundreds of millions of images it still matters, since it sets how much the captions cost to generate. We measured it only for the three candidates, all served through vLLM with no quantization or custom kernels. The tuning was at the pipeline level: one vLLM replica per GPU, with enough Ray Data pool workers to keep all eight GPUs on a node saturated. We first found Qwen3-VL-8B to be the fastest (20 img/s per H200) and chose it, for its speed, quality, and stable, release-grade vLLM support. Only later did we find that the Qwen2.5-VL "Relaxed" captioner reaches the same 20 img/s once fixed: it had been saved with the wrong architecture class, which broke vLLM's torch.compile hashing and forced slow eager mode until we re-saved it as Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration. Qwen3.5-9B produces great captions but ran slower (~6.5 img/s) and needed unstable nightly dependency builds at the time. A few months on, it is probably a great choice too.

At the end of the pipeline, we turn the captioned, bucketed stream into MDS, the format the trainer streams.

The Mosaic Streaming library packs samples into ~128MB shards streamed during training from object storage or a local filesystem. Lance does support simple distributed training as well, but we found that converting to MDS is the lower friction path for us. Mosaic Streaming gives us, for free, the distributed-training machinery we'd otherwise have to build ourselves:.

Industry observers note that diffusion training runs on fixed-size tensors, so every image in a batch must share one width and height. Rather than crop everything square (losing the sides of portraits and landscapes) or pad (wasting compute), we use aspect-ratio bucketing: a small set of allowed (w, h) shapes, with each image snapped to the nearest one and only same-shape images batched together.

Recent findings suggest that we bucket in two steps. First by resolution tier (pixel count): a 512px and a 1024px tier for most of the corpus, plus 2048px and 4096px tiers for high-resolution data. An image goes into the largest tier it can reach without upscaling by more than 4/3 (~33%), so each tier's floor is (size × 3/4)² (≈384² for the 512 tier, 768² for 1024); anything below the smallest floor is dropped. Then by aspect ratio within the tier: we enumerate the patch-aligned (w, h) shapes (both divisible by 16, AR in [0.5, 2.0]) that keep a roughly constant ~256-patch token budget, giving 13 buckets per tier, from 0.5 (tall) through 1.0 (square) to 2.0 (wide). At 512px that's 352×704 … 512×512 … 704×352; at 1024px the same 13 ratios scaled up. Constant patch count keeps per-image compute flat across shapes.

Each image is then resized to its bucket with a Lanczos filter and encoded as JPEG at quality 92, and Mosaic Data Shards are written into a tree keyed by resolution and aspect ratio so the trainer can stream buckets separately:.

In a recent development, the exploration in Section 2 relied on whatever captions a dataset shipped with. Once our own detailed captions were in place, the same full-text search became far more powerful, and a few passes over the captions turned up things the sparser original metadata had hidden: more text-heavy images (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics) than we had estimated, and some NSFW content that had slipped through.

In a recent development, to turn those approximate searches into a filter, we ran a quick classification pass with Qwen3-8B in text-only mode: it reads each caption (never the image) and labels the sample visual, text, or nsfw. The whole heuristic is essentially one question, "Would you look at this image, or read it?" Classifying from the caption rather than the pixels is cheap (around 200 captions/s per GPU) and reuses work we had already done. A pixel-level image classifier would likely be more accurate, but this was good enough to remove the obvious cases at moderate cost and without having to annotate data and train a custom classifier.

Rather than rewrite the whole corpus to drop these samples, we added a skip-list feature to the MDS data loader: a small sidecar file per shard lists the sample indices to skip, and the loader unions them and skips those samples at training time. Nothing is deleted or rewritten. This turned out to be a flexible mechanism well beyond this one filter. We can exclude any set of examples identified after the fact, whether a newly discovered quality glitch, a blacklist, or, importantly, data from consumers who later opt out of having their content used for training, simply by extending the skip list before the next run. It is also convenient for ablations: to measure a filter's effect, train once with the skip list and once without, off the same dataset, instead of storing two copies. The one limit is scale. Skip lists add a little per-sample work at load time, so once the skipped fraction grows large (we would estimate somewhere around 10%, though we have not measured the crossover), it becomes worth rewriting the MDS dataset without the skipped samples rather than carrying an ever-growing skip list.

Recent findings suggest that the same explorer surfaced a fair number of duplicates: large image collections tend to accumulate exact and near-duplicate copies, which waste training compute and skew the distribution. We mainly targeted near-duplicates and exact copies, so we added a quick deduplication pass using perceptual hashes. If the goal is to identify duplicate concepts and balance them in a dataset, deduplication based on clusters of image embeddings is a more suitable approach.

Industry observers note that we could have done an exact dedup on a byte hash like SHA-256, but a perceptual hash already subsumes that (it matches byte-identical images too) while also catching re-encoded or resized copies, so we used only the perceptual hash. It is a standard DCT-based perceptual hash (downscale to a small grayscale thumbnail, 2D DCT, threshold the low-frequency coefficients into a compact fingerprint), implemented in a few lines on top of OpenCV and SciPy. We consider two hashes a match if their Hamming distance is zero, so we only remove near-pixel-identical copies. Genuinely different shots of the same subject have different fingerprints (and different captions) and are kept on purpose.

It has been revealed that once every image has a perceptual hash (fingerprint), the dedup itself is just a hash-map lookup: scanning each aspect-ratio bucket across resolutions, we keep one entry per fingerprint, so any image whose fingerprint we have already seen is a duplicate of the one we kept, and when a cluster spans resolutions we keep the highest-resolution copy. The duplicates are written out as a per-shard skip list that the loader unions and skips at load time, so nothing is deleted and the dataset is never rewritten.

Across the corpus, deduplication removed on the order of a few percent of images, the caption-based text filter a few percent more, and the NSFW pass a small fraction of a percent.

The dataset described here is the pre-training corpus, where breadth and scale matter most. For supervised fine-tuning and preference alignment the trade flips entirely: quality matters far more than quantity, and the problem becomes finding and curating small, high-signal subsets out of this large corpus. To do that we have been building more powerful curation tooling, including a richer explorer that tags images with structured attributes predicted by a VLM so we can assemble highly targeted subsets for fine-tuning. We initiative to dig into topics like fine-tuning and preference alignment as well as the data tooling we use for these in a future post.

Sources indicate that build something with PRX, or find a bug in our pipeline? PRX is Apache 2.0 and the model code lives at github.com/Photoroom/PRX. We integrated PRX into the diffusers library and there is a Hugging Face Space to try out our latest version PRX Pixel.

arXiv:2607.29519v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Context: Graduate students in computing now use Large Language Models (LLMs) throughout their research, from literature reviews and coding to data analysis and writing. Objective: We investigate which LLM-based practices graduate students employ in their research and which skills they need to benefit from these practices. Method: We conducted a grey literature review of Reddit discussions. We retrieved 1,383 posts from five research-oriented subreddits, screened them against explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria, and analyzed the 54 included posts with thematic analysis, in which two authors independently coded each excerpt. Results: We identified seven categories of practices and nine categories of skills. Commenters locate the problem in accepting generated output without inspection rather than in using LLMs, and warn that delegating the effortful parts of a task, such as debugging, reading, or validating sources, delivers the output without building the skill the task was meant to develop. Traditional skills, such as programming and critical thinking, are what allow students to verify what an LLM produces. Conclusions: Our categories give graduate programs a concrete basis to teach students to work with LLMs without eroding the skills that research training should build, and they add research-specific skills, such as data sharing and scientific reproducibility, to existing AI competency frameworks.

Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

Parallel schedules split candidates into groups and advance a fixed quota from each. When a group holds more of the top passages than its quota, some are cut, and expensive repair calls become required. We show that the way candidates are split matters where such a quota can bind, and that, in expected cuts, the best split there deals them round-robin by retriever rank, like cards. Although not conceptually new, dealing has remained unanalyzed. We prove that, under a simple retriever model, no split with equal quotas cuts fewer of the true top ten on average, and that contiguous chunks cut more as the retriever improves. DealRank, the simplest schedule our analysis allows, is on average within 0.1 nDCG@10 points of the best schedules over six LLMs, in two rounds. It is consistently 1.1 to 1.4 times faster than BlitzRank with concurrent first calls up to a thousand candidates. There, it needs three rounds and is eleven times faster than the sliding window. In existing schedules such as BlitzRank, dealing reduces repair calls from 59% of queries to 14%, improving latency with no significant change in quality. Random partitioning appears equivalent at a quota of four, as predicted, but ties results to the seed and trails by 1.3 nDCG@10 points at a quota of one over a dense retriever.

We evaluate repair risk on Deribit BTC and ETH option chains, using $L_1$ and $L_2$ projections of midpoint prices onto the same admissible set as matched controls. Across 108 matched evaluations spanning 18 sampled calendar months, the median 90th percentile of the scaled spot-gamma gap for $L_2$ versus the $\rho=10$ smoothness-penalized repair is nearly twenty times the matched $L_1$--$L_2$ control. We also instantiate NN-Proj, a neural-projection repair, to test whether learned repairs exhibit repair risk. Despite good held-out fit, its downstream outputs remain distinct from those of classical repairs. Across five seeds with the same training window and architecture, its curvature dispersion exceeds the matched $L_1$--$L_2$ control in 17 of 18 months ($p=1.45\times10^{-4}$). For a USD 1 million risk reversal, switching from $L_2$ to the $\rho=10$ repair shifts the median 90th-percentile hedge notional by 18.62 basis points of gross spot notional. VaR-style estimates also exhibit greater dispersion across repairs. The repair rule is therefore part of the risk model, not merely a feasibility check.

arXiv:2607.23624v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.

arXiv:2611.20821v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) safety evaluation typically assigns each prompt or image a single culture-blind harm label, so content that is harmful only within a particular culture can pass as benign. We introduce CultureCraft, an agentic framework that constructs T2I prompts that appear benign under a general-purpose rubric yet carry a latent harmful meaning in a target culture, and use it to build CuRSE-Bench: 10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 culture-general controls over six regions and ten harm axes, each drawn from a predefined knowledge base of documented harm vectors and traceable to at least two independent sources. Scoring every prompt under six region persona judges and a paired culture-blind judge, we find that the culture-blind judge under-rates culture-specific latent harm while matching the persona judges on the controls. Each persona judge, in turn, chiefly decodes its own region's latent harm under our instrument: a selective cultural blind spot that persists in deployed moderators.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.22367v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot failures are difficult to collect at scale, limiting the range of failure scenarios represented in robot learning datasets. We present FailureGen, a method for generating synthetic videos with temporal event annotations by reusing action trajectories from recorded failures. The method comprises four stages: (1) fine-tuning an action-conditioned Cosmos world model on successful and failed real executions; (2) annotating source recordings to identify failure-associated donor segments and compatible successful hosts; (3) transferring donor motion into host contexts, with optional spatial offsets, to generate continuous video rollouts; and (4) annotating and filtering the generated samples according to observed events and visual quality. We study two implementations with different tasks and robot configurations, with visual failure detection serving as one downstream application. In a preliminary comparison, a detector trained on real and generated data achieves an average precision of 0.51, compared with 0.41 using real data alone, and detects 33 of 36 failure intervals, compared with 28 of 36. By reusing observed failures in additional contexts, FailureGen expands the data available for studying robot failures and developing downstream learning methods.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.20719v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Visuomotor policies condition action prediction on visual and proprioceptive observations. While historical proprioceptive sequences carry rich dynamic priors, current methods treat them as equal to high-dimensional vision, causing the proprioceptive signal to be overwhelmed. To identify what is lost in equal-conditioning fusion, we analyze proprioceptive data and find that strong inter-joint coupling is the key action-determining structure. This finding aligns with the neural sensorimotor loop, in which proprioception first forms a body-centered prior and vision is later calibrated via parietal remapping. Inspired by this, we propose ACiT, Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers, which reinforces historical joint-coupling as the primary condition with vision as a later calibration. This design is instantiated through three modules: Inverted State Encoding builds a proprioceptive prior via per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention. State-Visual Grounding lets joint tokens query visual evidence, making vision goal- and calibration-only. Inverted Action Chunking decodes per-joint trajectories independently. ACiT improves success rates on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, with the largest gains on those that require dynamics and coordination. The same conditioning design transferred to the VLA backbone pi_0-ACiT yields significant gains with better execution efficiency.

#20824. LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

📅 07 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1757 w)

LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

📅 07 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This upcoming release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all.
  • LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of fresh VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward).
  • The robotics world is asking a big question: do world models actually help robot policies?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This upcoming release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all. It also brings depth sensing, VLM-powered dataset annotation, custom video encoding, cloud training on HF Jobs, and a much leaner install.

LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of fresh VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward). It ships six new simulation benchmarks unified under lerobot-eval, the lerobot-rollout CLI with DAgger-style human-in-the-loop corrections, FSDP training, and cloud training on HF Jobs. Datasets get depth support, an automatic language annotation pipeline, custom video encoding, and up to 2x faster data loading, all on top of a leaner installation.

The robotics world is asking a big question: do world models actually help robot policies? v0.6.0 brings three policies to LeRobot to help answer that question. Each one learns to imagine the future as part of its training, and each takes a different path to keep that imagination affordable.

According to recent reports, VLA-JEPA teaches a compact VLA (built on Qwen3-VL-2B) to predict the future in latent space while it learns to act: during training, a JEPA world model has to anticipate upcoming frames from the model's own actions. The trick is that the world model then disappears at inference, so you get world-model supervision at zero extra inference cost. Three ready-to-use checkpoints are on the Hub, including a DROID-pretrained base for fine-tuning:.

Check out the VLA-JEPA documentation and the paper to learn more.

In a recent development, lingBot-VA goes one step further: an autoregressive video-action model that predicts future video and actions together, chunk by chunk, and feeds real observations back in to keep its imagination grounded. You can even save what the robot imagined (--policy.save_predicted_video=true) and compare it with what actually happened. Inference runs on a single 24–32 GB GPU. Check out the documentation and the paper for the technical details.

It has been revealed that fastWAM asks the question in its paper title: do world action models need test-time future imagination? It pairs a ~5B video-generation expert with a compact action expert in a single network, so the model literally learns to dream its own rollouts. At inference it skips the dreaming entirely and directly denoises action chunks. Fine-tune it from lerobot/fastwam_base, and read more in the documentation.

We upgraded our NVIDIA GR00T integration to GR00T N1.7, the newest open generation of NVIDIA's cross-embodiment foundation model. N1.7 swaps the previous VLM for Cosmos-Reason2-2B (built on Qwen3-VL) feeding a flow-matching action head, and our integration is parity-tested against NVIDIA's original Isaac-GR00T implementation: same inputs, same outputs. Flash-attention is now optional, so pip install 'lerobot[groot]' just works, and you can load NVIDIA's published checkpoints directly.

According to recent reports, GR00T N1.7 replaces N1.5 in LeRobot. If you need N1.5, pin lerobot==0.5.1.

MolmoAct2, the Allen Institute for AI's vision-language-action model, is now ported into LeRobot with the full lifecycle covered: fine-tuning (full or LoRA), evaluation, and real-robot deployment. Ready-made checkpoints with calibration correction baked in mean you can run it zero-shot on an SO-100/101:.

Industry observers note that inference fits in ~12 GB at bf16, and LoRA fine-tuning fits on a single 24 GB GPU. See the MolmoAct2 documentation for the full deployment guide.

Sources indicate that EO-1, a VLA pretrained upstream on interleaved vision-text-action data, joins LeRobot: a Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone with a flow-matching action head, contributed by one of the paper's own authors. Train it with the standard lerobot-train workflow using --policy.type=eo1. Details in the documentation and the paper.

It has been revealed that the Multitask Diffusion Transformer policy brings the TRI Large Behavior Models recipe to LeRobot: a ~450M-parameter diffusion transformer conditioned on CLIP vision and language embeddings, so one model learns many tasks selected via natural language. It supports both diffusion and flow-matching objectives, and it is small enough to train yourself. See the documentation.

Recent findings suggest that VLAs don't have to be huge. EVO1 packs its policy into 0.77B parameters, an InternVL3-1B backbone with a flow-matching action head, small enough to fine-tune and run in real time on modest GPUs. It ships with two-stage fine-tuning and Real-Time Chunking support out of the box. See the EVO1 documentation and the paper.

Success detection and progress estimation are missing pieces in the robot learning loop, and v0.6.0 gives them a home. LeRobot now has a unified reward models API (lerobot.rewards), mirroring the policies API, with four reward models behind one interface - the HIL-SERL reward classifier, SARM, and two new additions:.

In a recent development, robometer is a pretrained, general-purpose reward model: point lerobot/Robometer-4B at any LeRobot dataset and it scores task progress and success from raw video plus a language instruction, with no task-specific training required. It is built on Qwen3-VL-4B and trained via trajectory comparisons over a dataset of more than one million robot trajectories (RSS 2026 paper).

Industry observers note that TOPReward goes fully zero-shot: no reward weights at all. It wraps an off-the-shelf VLM (Qwen3-VL) and reads the log-probability of the token "True" given the trajectory video and the task instruction. Any capable VLM becomes a reward function.

According to recent reports, both ship with labeling scripts that write per-frame progress curves into your dataset, ready for reward-aware behavior cloning (RA-BC), dataset quality inspection, and progress-overlay videos. Check the Robometer and TOPReward docs.

Recording is no longer stuck with one hard-coded codec. The new --dataset.rgb_encoder.* options expose the full encoding surface (codec, quality, pixel format, GOP, presets), and vcodec=auto probes for hardware encoders like NVENC, VideoToolbox, VAAPI, and QSV before falling back to the default software AV1 encoder. For existing datasets, one command re-encodes everything:.

Full details in the video encoding documentation.

Industry observers note that plug in an Intel RealSense, set use_depth: true, and LeRobot records depth maps end to end: captured in millimeters, compressed as compact 12-bit depth video streams alongside your RGB cameras, and decoded back to physical units at training time. Depth renders live during recording and in lerobot-dataset-viz, and it works across SO-100/101, Koch, OpenArm, reBot, Unitree G1 and more.

Sources indicate that your dataset stops being one task string per episode. LeRobot datasets now natively store rich language annotations (timestamped subtasks, plans, memory, corrections, speech, and per-camera VQA pairs), and the latest lerobot-annotate CLI fills them in automatically using a VLM that watches your episodes:.

A YAML recipe layer then renders these annotations into chat-style training messages at sample time: exactly the data tomorrow's long-horizon, talking robot policies will train on. Scale it up with HF Jobs, and read the annotation pipeline docs to learn more.

In a recent development, training on video datasets is now up to ~2x faster out of the box: multi-camera frames decode in parallel, dataloader workers ship compact uint8 frames (4x less memory between processes), and persistent workers keep decoder caches alive across epochs. Loading a subset of a large dataset (episodes=[...]) went from minutes to milliseconds (275 s down to 0.06 s in our benchmark). Sampling is also deterministic and resumable now, so interrupted trainings restart sample-exact.

v0.5.0 planted the flag on LeRobot as an evaluation hub for VLAs; v0.6.0 makes it the real deal with six new simulation benchmarks, all runnable through the same lerobot-eval CLI, each with a docs page, a Docker image, and a SmolVLA baseline checkpoint smoke-tested in CI:.

Simulator backends require specific system dependencies with their own install steps; each docs page has the exact recipe, and every benchmark ships a ready-made Docker image if you'd rather skip the setup.

Together with LIBERO, Meta-World, and NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, that makes nine benchmark families under one roof, and a fresh Adding a New Benchmark guide documents exactly how to plug in yours. Evaluation also got faster: parallel eval now defaults to async vectorized environments, benchmarked at up to 2x faster.

Deploying a policy used to be a hack on top of lerobot-record. The latest lerobot-rollout CLI makes deployment its own workflow, with pluggable strategies and inference backends (including Real-Time Chunking for slow compatible VLAs). The base strategy just runs the policy. sentry records continuously, rotating episodes and uploading to the Hub as it goes. highlight keeps a ring buffer and saves the last N seconds when you hit a key, so an interesting moment is never lost. episodic mirrors the classic episode/reset recording workflow. And dagger turns deployment into data collection.

With the DAgger strategy, you watch your policy run, hit a key (or a USB foot pedal) the moment it goes wrong, take over with your leader arm to record the correction, and hand control back. Actuated leaders are driven to the follower's pose before you take over, so the handover is jerk-free. Every correction frame is tagged with an intervention flag, and the resulting dataset is ready for the next fine-tune:.

Deploy, collect corrections, fine-tune, repeat: the robot learning flywheel is now a CLI flag. Read the deployment docs.

Robot foundation models are outgrowing single GPUs. LeRobot training now supports FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) through Accelerate: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state are sharded across GPUs, and checkpoints are gathered back into a plain single-file model.safetensors that loads like any other policy. You can even resume an FSDP run on a different number of GPUs. See the multi-GPU training docs.

Sources indicate that no GPU? No problem. The exact same lerobot-train command now runs in the cloud by adding one flag:.

Industry observers note that leRobot pushes your local dataset to a private Hub repo if needed, submits the job, streams logs to your terminal, and pushes the trained policy to the Hub at the end. Pick anything from a T4 to 8x H200 with --job.target (compute is billed pay-as-you-go). Check out the documentation.

Check the release notes for the full list and migration pointers for the breaking changes.

Beyond these headline features, v0.6.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, and quality-of-life upgrades across the codebase, from smarter defaults to more reliable CI.

In a recent development, we want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community. This release includes work from academia, industry and hobbyists teams who chose LeRobot as the home for their models and benchmarks. Every PR and bug report pushes open-source robotics forward.

Sources indicate that stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22444v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2605.12925v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluation of software engineering (SWE) agents is dominated by a binary signal: whether the final patch passes the tests. This outcome-only view treats a principled solution and a chaotic trial-and-error process as equivalent. We show that this equivalence is empirically false. We evaluate 2,614 OpenHands trajectories from eight model backends on 60 SWE-bench Verified tasks. Of these, 47 have enough passing trajectories to construct task-level process references, yielding a 1,815-trajectory evaluation subset. Among passing trajectories in this subset, 10.7% exhibit behavior we call a Lucky Pass: regression cycles, blind retries, missing verification, or temporally disordered exploration, implementation, and verification. We introduce AgentLens, a framework for process-level assessment of SWE-agent trajectories, and release AgentLens-Bench, a dataset of 1,815 trajectories annotated with quality scores, waste signals, divergence points, and 47 task-level Prefix Tree Acceptor (PTA) references. AgentLens builds PTA references by merging multiple passing solutions for the same task, and uses a context-sensitive intent labeler to assign actions to Exploration, Implementation, Verification, or Orchestration based on trajectory history rather than tool identity alone. On AgentLens-Bench, the quality score separates passing trajectories into Lucky, Solid, and Ideal tiers and further decomposes Lucky Passes into five recurring mechanisms. Across the eight model backends, Lucky rates range from 0.5% to 23.2%, and some models move by as many as five rank positions when ranked by quality score instead of pass rate. We publicly release AgentLens-Bench and the AgentLens SDK at https://github.com/agentlens-framework/agentlens, with a project page at https://agentlens-framework.github.io/agentlens/.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22543v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual world models predict future visual states conditioned on actions, but recursive errors in entity poses and spatial relations limit their long-horizon prediction for robot planning and control. We ask whether a separately predicted relational state can correct this drift without restructuring the visual model. This is challenging because graph nodes and visual states share neither elements nor a feature space. We propose Joint Graph--Visual Dynamics Correction (JointGV), a plug-in based on a cross-granularity dynamics hypothesis: despite their different representations, graph-node and visual-state changes describe the same physical transition. JointGV rolls out a task-conditioned scene graph alongside the visual world model, couples their predicted changes, and combines the resulting graph-motion context with graph-predicted node positions to compute a bounded residual. Graph-learning and correction gradients do not propagate into the original visual dynamics. We attach JointGV to DINO-WM (spatial tokens) and DreamerV3 (a global latent state), evaluating both on DMC Cheetah Run and Walker Walk across three seeds and extending the evaluation to contact-rich manipulation with DMC Finger Turn Hard. Across 32-step rollouts, JointGV improves structural and visual-prediction accuracy, reducing joint-position error by 11--28\%. For spatial tokens, learned graph--visual change coupling gives lower error than broadcasting the same mean graph-motion context to every token, particularly when non-adjacent parts appear close together in the image. On real-robot inverted-pendulum sequences, JointGV reduces DINO-WM's 32-step pole-angle error from $12.56^\circ$ to $6.69^\circ$ and improves DreamerV3 and LeWorldModel as well. In simulated inverted-pendulum control, an actor trained with JointGV-corrected rollouts completes 46 of 50 episodes, compared with none using the original rollouts.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.20718v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich manipulation, yet heterogeneous sensing mechanisms and observation formats hinder cross-hardware transfer. Since physical contact is governed by Newtonian mechanics, we ground tactile representations in six-dimensional wrenches, establishing a common physical reference across sensing mechanisms. Specifically, we pair tactile observations from all sensors with wrench measurements, enabling shared physical supervision without requiring direct tactile-to-tactile pairing between sensors. To support learning at scale, we develop a dedicated acquisition platform and collect over 100 million paired tactile observations and wrench measurements from 24 sensors spanning four families of sensing principles. Building on this dataset, our framework combines sensor-specific input adaptation with a shared tactile encoder. By learning to reconstruct wrenches, the encoder maps observations from different sensors into a shared, continuous feature space grounded in contact physics. To leverage these representations for manipulation, we introduce TaF-Policy, which integrates tactile features with visual observations and robot states to generate action chunks. We evaluate the learned representations through wrench estimation, cross-sensor retrieval, few-shot adaptation to unseen sensors, and robotic manipulation. On the core benchmark, our method reduces single-frame force RMSE by 17.1% and improves cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13.11 percentage points over the strongest baseline. In manipulation experiments, TaF-Policy achieves average success rates of 51.33% across three simulated tasks and 46.25% across four real-world tasks, compared with 47.33% and 23.75%, respectively, for the strongest baselines evaluated on the same task sets. Project page: https://mrjiangjm.github.io/TaF-Foundation/.

arXiv:2611.19273v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) has recently attracted interest because it provides dense teacher guidance without a separate, often larger teacher model. However, OPSD conditions its teacher on ground-truth solutions, which limits its use when such solutions are unavailable. We propose On-Policy Self-Distillation with Self-Generated Problem Briefs (B-OPSD). Using a prompt template, the initial model or a saved student checkpoint generates a problem brief from the question alone. The prompt asks for relevant principles, applicability conditions, and likely pitfalls, but not a final answer or a complete solution. A frozen teacher uses the brief as privileged context to guide the current student's on-policy rollouts through token-level distribution matching. B-OPSD uses no ground-truth solutions during training. Results on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 show that both B-OPSD variants achieve higher average accuracy than OPSD at each of three Qwen3 model sizes. Code is available at https://github.com/ZevineXu/B-OPSD.

Breaking: The Best Smart Bird Feeders for Backyard Birding (2026)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one.
  • It has been revealed that to answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints.
  • Updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a new Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You’ve probably seen a smart bird feeder or know someone who has one. The best smart bird feeders are easily recognizable with their clear housing, cameras, and solar panels. Perhaps a friend or family member has sent you a photo or video of a bright goldfinch or a handsome woodpecker (guilty). But are these feeders really worth their $100-plus price tag? Are they durable? And what about the squirrel problem?

It has been revealed that to answer these questions, I’ve been testing the most popular smart bird feeders, including models from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, for more than two years—in rain, snow, and heat, and in a yard with persistent varmints. I’ve explored the apps and notification settings, examined the photo and video quality, noted which features are hidden behind a subscription paywall, and used Cornell Lab’s All About Birds—as well as Google Lens and my own expertise—to verify the accuracy of AI identifications. The recommendations below are what I would buy with my own money, having tested dozens of brands and models for a minimum of four weeks each.

Updated November 2026: I’ve added the Birdbuddy Nook as a new Best Budget pick, Kiwibit's Feeder 2 Pro as an Honorable Mention, and information on Birdfy's rollout of free AI ID. I've also removed a couple of discontinued feeders and updated links and prices.

According to recent reports, this cheery blue- or yellow-roofed feeder, from security company Netvue, was the first smart feeder WIRED tested, back in 2022, when it earned a 6/10 rating due to its high price and wonky AI. Both metrics have improved dramatically since then—Birdfy's app is now the second-most user-friendly on the market, behind only Birdbuddy's, and this feeder is often on sale for around $130. Its AI identification, which is decent, used to be paywalled but is now free with every tier of feeder.

In a recent development, the 1080p/2K camera isn't the best quality you'll find, but it does have one of the widest viewing angles of any smart feeder, at 155 degrees, so you're more likely to get full bird shots, as opposed to just heads and butts. The plastic housing (available in blue or yellow) also makes this feeder durable and easy to clean, and the 50-ounce seed reservoir is super easy to fill with its convenient flip-up top. Not all bundles come with a solar panel, but you can buy one separately. Unlike with other feeders, the solar panel is not built in and needs to be mounted and connected separately with the included 9.8-foot charging cable.

It's not the fanciest feeder on the market, nor the one with the best camera, but I've never had a problem with the two models I've been rotating in and out throughout the years, and the reliability and price point make it the best bet for most backyard birders.

Target (Solar + Extended Perch).

Birdbuddy's brand-new Nook model is a lot of bird feeder for the price; it won our recent head-to-head test of sub-$100 smart feeders. The base $99 model doesn't come with a solar roof or extended perch, as seen in the photo above, but you will get a 2K HDR camera that can shoot vertically or horizontally (it pops in and out via a magnet), as well as the same sturdy, high-quality construction as Birdbuddy's pricier Home model. The seed capacity isn't the greatest at 0.9 liters, but the app is easy to use and can even identify birds nearby that don't land on the feeder, so long as its excellent onboard microphone hears their sounds.

Recent findings suggest that birdbuddy's Achilles’ heel has always been its sensor, which is slow to wake up and regularly misses bird visits. The fresh Birdbuddy feeder supposedly has a faster wake-up time than previous models, and though it still lagged behind Birdfy's competing Rookie feeder in capturing all visits, the Nook's rate was substantially better than the Home's. It also has more mounting options, allowing for hanging in addition to wall and pole mounts (though the latter is a loose fit), and allows for no-cost manual AI ID of all visitors.

In a recent development, camojojo's original Hibird feeder has long been a reliable model in my testing stable, one of the first to run on both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi bands, and last year saw the debut of an upgraded model, the Hibird Pro. The enhancement has built-in solar panels, an option for pole-mounting, and supposedly improved AI identification, though it still frequently misidentifies even common birds in my West Coast backyard as East Coast species. The app is not as streamlined or user-friendly as Birdfy's or Birdbuddy's, but it's still easy enough to navigate, with options for changing video length (default is 10 seconds) or viewing in slo-mo. The default media type it saves is video, though this is 4K Ultra HD, and the images are—as expected—extremely sharp. Without a subscription, you can't search past videos by bird, and cloud storage is capped at 5 GB over 60 days; however, the feeder does come with a 128-GB SD card. You'll also get “smarter” chats with the app's AI Q&A function, “Dr. Bird,” and the ability to share across two devices with a subscription ($45 per year or $4 per month).

Recent findings suggest that I appreciate the generous 1.5-liter seed hopper, although this, combined with the solar panel and battery, makes it extremely heavy. When filled, it tips the scales at 5 pounds, meaning that if you do pole-mount it, you will need to use both included hose clamps and wrench them tightly. I also wouldn't attempt to mount it on anything unstable, like a wobbly fence. Other original Hibird features that made it to the Pro include the little handles on the assembly screws (so you won't need any assembly tools) and the chunky plastic body. The latter was subjected to a little bit of squirrel-chewing during my test, but it still held up well.

In a recent development, the Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 is one of the most thoughtfully designed feeders on the market. You don't have to take down the whole feeder when refilling, as the 1.5-liter dual-hopper plastic seed reservoir is removable from the body. The 8-megapixel photos and 4K HD video have much better quality than you'll find from most competitors, and the components come apart for easy cleaning. I also tested the original version, which features a separate solar panel, and my only complaint was that the panel stopped charging the camera after about six weeks. This version features a built-in solar roof, which did an excellent job keeping the feeder charged during its six-week-long test, even on cloudy days. The plastic body is extremely thick and sturdy, and unlike lighter-weight feeders like Birdfy's, it's designed to hold up in more extreme weather.

The app is easy to navigate, and the whole setup is functional without a Kiwibit Plus subscription ($90/year, purchasable online or through the Kiwibit app) but you'll be losing out on a lot of features, including 60-day storage and the ability to record up to three minutes of video if a bird is doing something interesting—a unique feature among smart feeders, and one I discovered that I love. (There's nothing more frustrating than having a video cut off right as a bird is about to do something funny.) This smart feeder costs a bit much for what it is, but if you know you like having a smart feeder, I think it's worth the investment. Note, however, that it only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi, and the warranty is half the length you get from many competitors. I also tested Kiwibit's newer model, the Feeder 2 Pro, and while its camera does have an interesting auto-zoom lens, I didn't think it was worth the $120 premium over this model.

It has been revealed that birdbuddy is known for its user-friendliness and thoughtful app—its Pro Smart Hummingbird Feeder is no exception. The feeder is intuitive and easy to use, and you don't need a subscription to access fun features like AI identification, 5 MP photos, and 2K HD video with slo-mo. A subscription unlocks features like family sharing and a higher bit rate, but the feeder is perfectly functional without those. With the panel being built into the feeder's roof, there’s also no auxiliary solar panel to worry about. Pairing with your phone is a cinch, integrating it into the Birdbuddy app with other feeders is a snap, and even refilling it is no problem. Unlike other hummingbird feeders that have weirdly cavernous capacities and/or need to be filled upside down, the Birdbuddy’s bottom screws off and holds a reasonable 1.75 cups of liquid. This detail is important; as the Cornell Lab of Ornithology points out, the easier it is to clean a hummingbird feeder, the more likely you are to do it often and well.

This feeder also comes with extra plastic flowers and a little brush for scrubbing them, and the app sends reminders when it's time to clean. You'll find fun, seasonal touches in the app, like the ability to send digital bird holiday cards with the photos your feeder captures, and a tool that superimposes hats, clothes, and various accessories on the birds, which is actually funnier than it sounds. However, as with the Birdbuddy seed feeders, the big downside is that the feeder's sensor doesn’t always pick up every bird that visits. This can definitely be a bummer, particularly when you see something interesting out the window but it doesn’t show up in the app.

After experiencing connection complications with the Birdfy Polygon, I swapped it out for the newer Birdfy Nest Duo and have had no issues. The sleek, contemporary Duo is a fir box fitted with two cameras—one facing the hole and one tucked discreetly inside the feeder. That gives you a full-spectrum view of what's going on. Both cameras have night vision (the internal one is infrared). Like the Polygon, the Duo sports a remote for rebooting and recharging the camera (though the separate solar panel, which can be pole-mounted, has kept the cameras reliably charged), as well as different-size holes for different species, each with its own chew-proof predator guard.

There's a metal grate with drainage holes that you can slot into grooves in the lower third of the Nest to make the cavity larger or smaller. The interested birds of my yard seemed very put off by the grate, so I covered it with a layer of craft mat moss, which was a success—a chickadee promptly moved in and laid seven eggs, all of which hatched. (I detail the experience in a separate review). For the first time, I was able to use the Birdfy app's ability to collect images from its nest boxes and string them together in a “story” that's shareable online. But I didn't find it especially useful or accurate. No matter, though, because the video captures have been a truly fascinating and educational experience, and I wish I could afford to buy the Duo for everyone I know.

Industry observers note that so far, the Duo has been rained on a bunch and survived a couple of heat waves, but the wood finish and black paint are peeling and will need refinishing before I put them up for next season. (The feeder comes equipped with a thermometer and hygrometer to keep an eye on conditions. I recently had to zip-tie an umbrella to mine during a heat wave, which likely saved some fledglings' lives, though the lightweight construction and black-painted side and top probably contributed to the box overheating.).

I rarely expect (or get) compliments on my backyard smart feeders, but I have gotten many on this one, which has a distinctively modern look with natural wood (bamboo that's FSC-certified to be responsibly sourced) and a black-painted side and roof. It blends right into the landscape as opposed to providing a visual pop of plastic. (The pole and baffle shown in the photo above are not included.).

In a recent development, birdfy's user-friendly app presents 2K HD images and video with free lifetime AI ID, and it's easy to share photos and videos with others. There's a solar panel you can mount separately, but I didn't do this and was impressed that the camera ran for nearly two months on an indoor USB-C charge.

Wood obviously comes with a higher risk of chewing by squirrels and other rodents, but there are metal guards available (both Birdfy-brand and aftermarket) that fit over the seed. I followed the 5-7-9 rule for pole-mounting to avoid this problem, but I was totally shocked at how weathered my feeder got after two months. And this was in a Pacific Northwest dry summer—about as mild as it gets. The finish was completely peeling off, so I recommend adding an extra layer of urethane (this is what I use) before putting it out for the first time, especially now, heading into winter.

Kiwibit’s new update to its original Feeder 2 is an interesting one; it’s the first bird feeder camera to feature autofocus in 4K HDR. The quality was exceptional, though, during my testing, some birds were alarmed by the camera movement. The biggest downside, though, is that most of this feeder’s features—including AI bird identification, expanded gallery views, and 60-day cloud storage—are now locked behind a $90-a-year paywall. It's not enough of an upgrade to justify paying the extra cash over the base-model Bird Feeder 2.

Sources indicate that A lower-maintenance way to enjoy birds in your yard, this recycled-plastic birdbath comes outfitted with a dual-lens camera sending 1080p photos and 2K video via the Birdfy app and using the app’s AI capability for (free) bird identification. With the IP66-rated birdbath’s sturdy metal base (you can buy it for less without) and solar-powered battery and fountain pump, all you have to do is make sure the 3.5-liter, 1.65-inch reservoir is topped off with water. I've been using the Bath Pro for two seasons now, and while early connection issues have been resolved, the plastic has weathered, and the pump only works intermittently. I also find myself increasingly irritated with how long footage takes to load and how often the shallow plastic basin needs refilling and cleaning—every two or three days in dry weather. Still, if you're willing to put up with some quirks, the Bath Pro has been an entertaining and welcome addition to my bird-feeding setup.

Sources indicate that birdfy's unique flagship upgrade for 2025 won a CES Innovation Award and an American Good Design Gold Award. It features one dual-lens front-facing camera (2-MP/1080p wide-angle and 3-MP/2K portrait) and one 2-MP/1080p side camera. Both capture sharp, highly detailed video with high-quality sound. The front-facing camera even pans and crops to ensure the lens is focused on a bird. (Note that there's also a cheaper, single-camera version of the Feeder 2 that we haven't tested.) The feeder's IP66-rated plastic body, which has held up very well in Pacific Northwest winter weather, is wall-, pole-, or tree-mountable. An auxiliary solar panel and lifetime AI bird identification are both included. The reservoir holds slightly less seed than the original plastic Birdfy, at 42 ounces versus Birdfy 1’s 50 ounces. Overall, I was impressed with both the image quality and the Birdfy app's updated AI identification. That remarked, both cameras repeatedly dropped connections during my two-month testing period, even though I was using the required 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi network (only the Birdfy Metal 2 can run on 5 GHz). The solar panel, which requires separate mounting, also failed to keep the cameras consistently charged in cloudy weather.

Plus, the 3-watt solar panel can mount onto the back for pole installation, and the 8-MP photos and 4K HD video are much higher quality than what you'll find from many competitors. However, it's still a good deal if you don't mind having to bring it inside every few weeks to charge.
