Like many inexpensive feeder cameras, most of the Harymor's advertised features—such as AI identification and the ability to take 2K video—are hidden behind a subscription paywall. However, even upon activating the subscription, the AI was wrong more often than it was right.

This feeder's got a generously sized dual-feed bay (4.2 cups on each side, for a total capacity of 8.4 cups); a built-in solar panel; an expandable perch; and a pretty solid 4-MP photo resolution, the clarity and quality of which were on par with more expensive cameras. There’s an option to view video in 0.5-speed slo-mo. As with most of the cheaper cameras, however, many of the features (like AI identification and video) are hidden behind a subscription. I didn’t find the ornithologist-trained AI identification to be super accurate, and the app was overall cumbersome to use, taking a while to load and then requiring multiple steps to engage the AI feature. I also didn't like that users must make an account that requires an address and phone number just to use the feeder, even if they’re not buying a premium plan. Industry observers note that I had high hopes for this feeder, my previous pick for Best Upgrade. Tool-free assembly, 4K ultrahigh-definition video, the ability to run on 2.4-GHz or 5-GHz Wi-Fi, a chew-proof metal body, and enhanced AI ID that is more accurate than the standard version and can even identify different sexes: The Metal 2 had it all. It even looks great, with tasteful green tones and a natural wood perch. However, I have now been through two test units, and both have repeatedly disconnected from Wi-Fi, despite being next to the wall closest to my router. (And I will note the feeders were located in the same spot where I test all the smart feeders; this issue is rare, but similar to my eventual experience with Birdfy's Polygon nest box and Duo feeder.).

Birdfy’s Hum Feeder Duo is the hummingbird-feeder version of the Duo seed feeder. Both editions of the Hum consist of a clear, BPA-free, anti-mold bottle that screws into a red base with a trio of plastic flowers. The duo has two 3-MP 2K cameras—one front-facing and one side-facing. The cameras charge together and provide a side-by-side view in the app. I had zero problems with setup. After an overnight charge, the feeder was up and running in about 10 minutes. One charge lasted a little over a week in Pacific Northwest November temperatures, though for $20 more, you can spring for the solar panel add-on with a patented ant moat (I have not yet tried this). I appreciate that the app demonstrates battery life alongside temperature and humidity, which is helpful for gauging when to replace the liquid, although a more explicit notification like Birdbuddy's would be helpful. Like the seed feeder, however, my testing period was not without issue. In fact, I only had the Hum up for a couple of weeks before the sensor appeared to have failed, occasionally capturing wind-driven motion but failing to register any birds.

Industry observers note that if you or a giftee is intimidated by the thought of a smart bird feeder, you may want to consider the Rookie. No complicated assembly, no solar panels, no tools—just snap three plastic pieces together, charge the camera, and you're ready to go. The whole setup reminds me of a gravity pet feeder. You'll have the same 1080p resolution as all other basic Birdfy cameras, but here the camera is mounted from the side. Half of the time, you'll only see a bird's back or butt. There's also no roof, meaning seeds will get wet in the rain (during my testing period, the lid even blew off with a gust of wind). You'll find some birds standing in the seed due to the lack of perch, which isn't great for disease spread. Battery life also wasn't stellar, down to 39 percent after only a week.

I love the style of this feeder, which looks like a contemporary condo and sports the same side-camera angle as the Rookie (left). Also like the Rookie, it's pretty simple—a 1080p camera and 1.3L seed hopper—and the camera angle ends up capturing a lot of bird butts. My main problem during the testing period, however, was durability. Birdfy doesn't specify the type of wood used in its construction, but it's very lightweight, almost like balsa wood. Even though I had it pole-mounted, it was knocked down and broken apart by squirrels within a week.

Just when I thought I'd seen it all in the smart bird feeder world, CoolFly debuted a feeder with a modular camera system at CES 2026. Place the camera on either side of the broad perch: upright for a landscape view or on its side for closer-up portrait images. When I tested it, I really liked the easy-fill seed hopper and tool-free assembly, paired with quality 4-MP photos and 2.5K Ultra HD video. I did not, however, love the incessant marketing push notifications in the CoolFly app. The Aura also sports AI ID without a subscription, but this feature only works in one of the two camera modes, neither of which was different enough from the other to justify the hassle of switching between them. I also had to remove the metal seed grate that sits on top, as smaller birds were struggling to access the seed. That stated, it's a perfectly fine feeder and was reliable in my tests, if you like the look.

It has been revealed that birdfy’s Polygon Smart Birdhouse is certainly unique-looking—the parallelogram-esque, turquoise-paneled shape won a Gold award at 2024’s French Design Awards—and it’s easy enough to mount on a pole, fence, or tree. All the camera equipment is located in an easy-to-open rear hatch, and there’s even a remote control at the end of a 10-foot cord to be able to charge or reset the 1080p camera (though it has a built-in solar panel, so I've never needed to do this). It's simple to integrate with the easy-to-use Birdfy app, which is ready and waiting to assemble a bird's shareable “story,” from building the nest to hatching to fledgling, and finally “the end,” when the nest is abandoned for the season. Note that the camera does emit an audible click whenever movement or the app triggers it, and when I had a chickadee interested in the nest, the bird clearly heard this and found it alarming. I have had consistent connectivity concerns over the two seasons I've used the Polygon, so if you're in the market for a smart nesting box, I recommend the Birdfy's Nest Duo instead, which is both more fun and more reliable for around $50 extra.

There is a subscription tier with features like increased storage and the ability to share livestreams, but the camera is still usable without it. What to Look for When Buying a Smart Bird Feeder.

In a recent development, the world of smart bird feeders is vast and can seem overwhelming, but there are some key features that will really make a difference in your user experience. I've tested dozens of feeders for years from many different brands, and this is what I think you should pay attention to when comparing models.

Subscription: Most, if not all, smart bird feeders require a subscription to access all features. That's in order to support the organization's continued investment in user experience. There are few things more disappointing than giving or receiving a smart bird feeder as a gift, only to find out it's not actually usable without shelling out an additional $70 a year. Reputable companies will note subscription requirements up front, and some even offer models that have a lifetime subscription built in. Note that if a feeder costs less than a hundred bucks, odds are it will require a subscription to capture photos, whether it says so in the marketing materials or not. You will need to do your due diligence before buying.

It has been revealed that mounting options: If you live in an area with squirrels, your best bet is to pole-mount your bird feeder—especially a more expensive smart feeder, which often has cords that squirrels and other rodents like to chew. Not all feeders offer a pole-mounting option, though, which is another notable detail to confirm before buying.

Sources indicate that wi-Fi network: The vast majority of smart feeders only work on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi frequencies. If you only use 5 GHz, you will need to look for a feeder that specifically works with a shorter transmission range or has dual range, such as the Camojojo Hibird, above.

App: An app can make or break your smart bird feeder experience since it's where all of your bird viewing, sorting, and saving will take place. Apps with added features like useful facts, the capacity to share feeds with others, quality AI identification, and the ability to sort by bird are sometimes worth the added cost over a less-expensive feeder. Many companies use security cameras in their bird feeders that don't have a separate app—this means you'll just get a utilitarian list of image captures with no detail or context. To help buyers with their decision-making, I am currently building a rubric to grade and rank smart bird feeder apps, which I hope to add to this guide within the next couple of months.

How Does WIRED Test Bird Feeders?

In a recent development, I test all feeders in my rural-suburban backyard in the Pacific Northwest. I mount seed feeders on a 1-inch pole with a baffle, using the provided mounting hardware and hose clamps. If pole-mounting isn't feasible, I mount on a fence or a shepherd's hook. I hang hummingbird feeders from a shepherd's hook mounted on the side of my house. I fill the seed feeders with Audubon Wild Park bird seed and the hummingbird feeders with a nectar mixture of 4-to-1 granulated sugar and water. I keep each feeder up for a minimum of four weeks, with all app notifications enabled.

I look at all app features available both with a subscription and without, seeing how often I get notifications and noting whether they are accurately picking up just birds or any type of outdoor movement, and how well the AI feature is able to distinguish bird species. I also look at connectivity, seed capacity, video quality, and how well the feeder bodies hold up to squirrels and inclement weather.

The majority of feeders I tested were provided as press samples by the organization. I keep some for longer-term testing, put others in storage for future testing or comparison purposes, and donate others locally via the Buy Nothing Project.

What Do I Need to Know Before Setting Up a Smart Feeder?

Why Do Most Smart Feeders Only Run on 2.4 GHz?

Sources indicate that this section was inspired by an email from a reader who installs home Wi-Fi systems and did not appreciate my recommending a feeder that has the option to run on 5 GHz. He's not wrong that this isn't the preferred band for a smart bird feeder, but I'll explain why someone might want 5 GHz below.

Recent findings suggest that first off, what is 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz? In simplest terms, these are the main radio frequency bands Wi-Fi uses to send data wirelessly between your smart bird feeder and your router. One gigahertz (GHz) is 1 billion hertz, the unit of measurement for how fast radio waves oscillate. Both bands are the accepted standards for Wi-Fi, which yes, is a name brand.

According to recent reports, it follows, then, that 2.4-GHz waves oscillate more slowly than 5-GHz waves. This also means the slower waves can travel farther and pass through walls and other obstacles more effectively. With Wi-Fi-enabled products placed outside the home, the ability to penetrate walls, trees, and other potential barriers is more important than speed. These slower waves also result in less power consumption by devices. It makes sense that 2.4 GHz would be a preferable band for a smart bird feeder, which likely would be in or near a tree-filled area.

However, 2.4 GHz is a more crowded band and thus prone to interference from other Wi-Fi networks and devices, so it can be less stable. It also results in slower overall performance, leading to sluggish downloads and lag during streaming and video calls. Most modern routers offer both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands, but some may be configured (for whatever reason) to broadcast only 5 GHz. Other routers feature something called band steering, which automatically diverts devices to the less-crowded 5 GHz. A smart bird feeder that offers dual connectivity simply provides more options. If the bird feeder is right outside your window where the router is located, you may want the faster speed. Or maybe you just don't want to try to figure out how to turn off band steering. If you're not dialed in to your router, no pun intended, it may make sense for you to consider a bird feeder with dual-band connectivity.

In a recent development, as is the case with any bird feeder, squirrels love to eat at smart bird feeders, most of which are not squirrel-proof, regardless of marketing claims. However, most of the smart feeders we’ve tested are just as sturdy, if not in some cases sturdier, than analog bird feeders. The worst-case scenario is likely the squirrel eating all the seed, chewing the edges, and covering up the camera with its fuzzy butt.

The yard where I test smart feeders year-round is lousy with the large and persistent rodents, and the squirrel damage I’ve sustained on test feeders has been minor. With the Birdfy Pro Duo, above, the animals chewed off the edges to better get at the seed supply when it was low, and the FeatherSnap Scout had its mounting bent. Top of mind is the 5-7-9 method of siting a bird feeder—at least 5 feet off the ground, at least 7 feet away from any structures, and at least 9 feet away from anything a squirrel could jump from (branches, fences, roofs). I explain this in more detail in my guide to keeping squirrels away from your bird feeder.

Another option is an aftermarket baffle added to feeders hanging on shepherd’s hooks, or a pole with a built-in baffle, like this one from Birdfy. Or you could use seed treated with capsaicin, or hot pepper. The taste doesn't affect birds, since they don’t have capsaicin receptors like mammals do. That noted, I’ve found capsaicin only keeps squirrels away for a couple of days, whether because they’ve gotten used to it or the pepper loses its potency when exposed to the elements. As a last resort, you could always just learn to live with the squirrels and dedicate a feeder to them, although my neighbor does this, and I'm of the mind that doing so brings even more squirrels to the area.

However, their discrete, non-linear behaviour makes them difficult to analyse and trust in safety-relevant settings. Existing approaches based on SAT and Satisfiability Modulo Theories can verify a BNN's input-output properties, but treat it as a monolithic constraint system, which reveal only whether a property holds and not how the computation reaches its result. In this paper, we present an early work that provides a complementary, discrete-event view. We give a compositional translation from the inference semantics of a fixed, trained BNN to a 1-safe Petri net (PN), where each computation step is an explicit transition, so that a firing sequence is a causal trace of the BNN's decision. On a worked example, we establish faithfulness via exhaustive input-output equivalence against a reference implementation, and show how contrasting firing sequences localises where a single-feature change alters the prediction. arXiv:2611.22588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In Mixed-Criticality (MC) systems, considering multiple Worst-Case Execution Times (WCETs) for the same task, corresponding to different system operation modes, presents a fundamental challenge in MC system design. Identifying suitable WCETs for lower (LO) criticality system operational modes is inherently difficult. Tight low WCET values may trigger frequent mode switches that degrade Quality-of-Service (QoS) by dropping/degrading the lower-criticality tasks and reducing their functionality. However, more conservative values reduce resource efficiency. Moreover, low WCET selection affects exposure assumptions under the adopted transient-fault model, which is used in reliability-aware scheduling analysis. Although some studies have considered low WCET determination to make a reasonable trade-off between processor utilization, mode switching probability and QoS, reliability constraints are typically addressed separately through fault-tolerance mechanisms. This separation overlooks the opportunity to use execution-time bounds as part of design-time reasoning about exposure-related reliability constraints. In this regard, we propose a reliability-aware analytical scheme, named ReBoT-MiCS, to determine low WCETs at design time, jointly balancing utilization, QoS, mode switches, and probabilistic reliability constraints of each task criticality level under a transient-fault exposure model. Experiments conducted with various synthetic and embedded benchmarks demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed scheme, in which utilization can be improved by up to 27.6% and 11.67% on average, while bounding the mode switching probability by up to 5.48%, and satisfying the specified reliability constraints.

Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud.
  • Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs.
  • Industry observers note that skyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

Industry observers note that skyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:.

In a recent development, that one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no latest storage account to create.

MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo indicates up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Sources indicate that authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

Sources indicate that GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every upcoming training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

In a recent development, to collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:.

Industry observers note that hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:.

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the new chunks leave the machine.

According to recent reports, add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

Sources indicate that the initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.

arXiv:2611.20710v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Reliable proprioceptive state estimation for legged robots fuses inertial sensing with kinematic sensing from leg encoders. The latter assumes a foot is stationary during the stance phase; however, physical foot touchdown does not necessarily provide a stationary reference for odometry, particularly during impact and load transfer. Repeatedly applying kinematic corrections throughout the same contact phase can introduce redundant or unreliable information. We present SG-ODOM, a proprioceptive odometry framework that uses stability-gated contact selection to schedule kinematic updates. Following physical touchdown, a stability gate accepts the contact for state estimation only after the foot reaches a sufficiently stable support condition. The resulting validated touchdown event triggers an estimator correction, while additional timeout updates bound the maximum duration of uninterrupted IMU propagation. The framework is evaluated on multiple legged platforms, both quadrupedal and humanoid robots, against representative state-of-the-art proprioceptive estimators. Across the evaluated sequences, SG-ODOM demonstrates competitive or superior estimation accuracy, reducing Relative Pose Error (RPE) by up to 25% compared to the baseline estimator on outdoor sequences from the GrandTour dataset. It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.22272v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transition states govern chemical reaction rates and outcomes, yet locating them remains a central challenge in computational chemistry. Double-ended search methods find transition states given reactant and product structures, but generally rely on discretized path representations developed for density functional theory, where potential energy surface evaluations are expensive. Machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) dramatically reduce this cost and leverage automatic differentiation to access higher-order derivatives efficiently. We introduce Popcornn, a framework to find transition states by optimizing continuous neural network paths atop an MLIP with a parallelized adaptive numerical integrator. This combination eliminates path discretization artifacts, reduces hyperparameter sensitivity, and enables non-local optimization to overcome local features using second-order potential-energy-surface information. Popcornn consistently recovers more correct transition states than standard methods such as nudged elastic band and growing string, across MLIPs on thousands of organic reactions, establishing it as a robust, automation-ready method for high-throughput transition state search. Popcornn's infrastructure is flexible in path objective, integration strategy, and optimization algorithm, making it a practical tool and platform for investigating open questions in MLIP-based path optimization.

arXiv:2611.22522v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The integrated analysis and optimisation codes used to design nuclear fusion reactors need to become increasingly large scale, multidisciplinary and complex to computationally verify design requirements more thoroughly and earlier in the design process. Though the manner in which the integrated models are coupled can have significant implications for computational efficiency, the structure of couplings typically remains hidden in the implementation of a design framework. As this problem is not unique to fusion, we frame integrated design problems as applications of the broader field of Multidisciplinary Design Analysis and Optimisation (MDAO). Originally developed for complex system design problems in e.g. aerospace, the MDAO field uses (extended) Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) to display the architecture of integrated analysis and optimisation codes. The aim of this work is to introduce these DSM methods and demonstrate how they can be used to improve the transparency and efficiency of design codes in fusion. As a proof of concept, DSM methods are applied to two case studies: stellarator optimisation with SIMSOPT and the PROCESS systems code. With these cases, we illustrate how a DSM can help identify structural assumptions in the code, and how architectural insight can be used to improve computational efficiency. In particular, we demonstrate the computational impact by modifying the PROCESS solver architecture based on the feedback loops revealed in an automatically generated DSM, yielding a significant reduction in model evaluations. Such architectural changes are considered especially impactful for future design frameworks that combine higher fidelity models with large numbers of inexpensive models.

Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (201 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22268v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.

As in Gueye and Jeanblanc (2022), the drivers may jump, so defaults may occur at stopping times of the reference filtration, including predictable ones, and a common jump may cause no, one or several simultaneous defaults. For general drivers, we derive the conditional joint survival law by a backward recursion; it is an explicit product of survival functions if and only if, for every set of names, the predictable reduction of the compensator of their first default time is deterministic. If, moreover, defaults avoid predictable stopping times, the law is a fatal shock law with hazards identified from the drivers; predictable default atoms can rule this out. Examples include L\'evy subordinators and, with random reductions but explicit laws, Liu's model and shot-noise drivers with memory.

However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At Microsoft Build 2026, we announced Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At Microsoft Build 2026, we announced Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute. Weights are pre-staged in Azure, runtimes are built and scanned by Microsoft, and every model in the Collection ships with the same enterprise security, governance, observability, and billing that applies to every other model on Foundry.

Microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications. Foundry starts with the widest model selection on any cloud — models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, and others, spanning frontier, open-source, and custom weights — all accessible through a single endpoint and a single set of SDKs in Python, C#, JavaScript, and Java.

On top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data. Once agents are running, Foundry provides end-to-end tracing, real-time monitoring, continuous evaluations, and a prompt optimizer that improves agent behavior based on eval results — observability and quality loops that are part of the platform.

Alongside that, developers get access to:.

Alongside pay-per-token (lowest-friction path to get started) and provisioned throughput (predictable, high-performance production workloads on frontier models), Foundry Managed Compute is the third deployment option in Foundry: a managed GPU platform-as-a-service for open-source and custom models.

You deploy a model instance described by the things that matter to your workload — parameter count, context length, and whether you want to optimize for latency or throughput — and Foundry handles the GPU topology underneath, whether the instance lands on one accelerator or several, so you think and plan in model terms.

Microsoft takes care of the machine: container updates, runtime upgrades, and security patches happen automatically on the supported runtimes — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, TEI, llama.cpp — without redeploying your model, while model configuration, deployment behavior, and routing stay with you.

That consistency carries through the developer surface — pay-per-token, provisioned throughput, and Managed Compute share:.

Open-source models integrate with Foundry Agents the same way frontier models do, so you can mix model types in a single agent without a separate integration path.

Recent findings suggest that same code, same workflow. Quota is aligned to accelerator families, so a initiative built on the H100 family today carries forward as latest hardware generations come online.

Hugging Face is the public square of open AI: 15 million builders, 400,000 organizations, and over 3 million open models published, with upcoming frontier capabilities — agentic coding, video segmentation, speech, embeddings — landing weekly. It's the GitHub of open models, where the community publishes weights, writes model cards, compares evaluations, and pulls models for experimentation.

Open models have closed the gap with proprietary models on benchmark after benchmark, and they unlock things proprietary endpoints can't:.

Industry observers note that the catch has always been the operational layer: discovery, license review, security screening, runtime selection, GPU sizing, image building, CVE patching, and standing the model up behind an enterprise-grade endpoint. Hugging Face, by itself, is not an enterprise serving platform. Hugging Face models on Foundry is that operational layer, run by Microsoft.

The Hugging Face Collection brings a curated subset of models directly into the Foundry Model Catalog:.

From your side, an open-weight model in the Hugging Face Collection looks and behaves like any other model in the Foundry Model Catalog, and every model in the Collection has been put through a multi-stage publishing pipeline before it ever reveals up there.

Hugging Face and Microsoft work together to bring the most popular open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem to Microsoft Foundry — production-ready for enterprise environments — through a systematic curation process:.

Because weights are pre-staged in Azure storage and runtime images live in a Microsoft-managed registry, your deployments won't need outbound network access to Hugging Face Hub — you can deploy to production inside a private network.

Hugging Face models on Foundry are powered by a versatile collection of community-built, open-source inference runtimes — each selected and tuned for Foundry Managed Compute, and matched to the model architectures it serves best. Across all runtimes, the systematic curation process means fresh versions and patches land on Foundry swiftly, and existing model deployments are upgraded automatically — without requiring you to redeploy.

Recent findings suggest that vLLM — the default high-throughput serving engine for open large language models, tuned for production GPU workloads. Because Hugging Face is a direct contributor to vLLM, any model in the Transformers library can run on vLLM out of the box — so when a fresh model lands on Hugging Face, it can be served on Foundry the same day, with no waiting on a custom integration.

Recent findings suggest that SGLang — a serving engine for language and multi-modal models, with strong support for structured outputs (JSON, regex, grammar-constrained generation) that agentic and tool-using workloads depend on. Hugging Face and the SGLang team have built a Transformers backend integration for SGLang, so any model in the Transformers library runs on SGLang out of the box — and reaches Foundry the same day it lands on Hugging Face.

Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) — the runtime for embedding, reranker, and sequence-classification models. Accelerator-specific images ship with kernels compiled for each GPU and CPU family Foundry supports, keeping the embedding hot path lean for RAG and semantic-search workloads.

llama.cpp — the CPU and small-GPU path for GGUF-quantized models. Useful for cost-optimized deployments, smaller models, and CPU-only regions, with the same OpenAI-compatible API as vLLM and SGLang.

TensorRT-LLM and NIM — used on NVIDIA hardware where NVIDIA's optimized kernels and Triton-based serving deliver meaningfully better latency or throughput for specific model families.

hf-serve — Hugging Face's own multi-model inference server, used for model architectures outside the LLM and embedding fast paths (vision, audio, segmentation, and other Transformers-native pipelines) so the Collection can cover every modality with a consistent serving layer.

The Hugging Face Collection in the Foundry Model Catalog is where you start, and deployment is five steps:.

A deployment template is the unit of choice in step 2: a named, versioned asset that pins the runtime, the accelerator family and count, the context length, and the runtime-specific tuning needed to serve the model well — so picking a template is the only knob you turn for "how do I want this model to run.".

qwen3-32b, for example, ships with four templates the deploy wizard exposes side by side:.

According to recent reports, each template arrives pre-tuned for the model — runtime settings, tool-call and reasoning parsers, scoring path, health probes, request concurrency, and any model-specific context-extension settings are all set by Microsoft, with any trade-offs called out inline in the template description. When you script the deploy, you reference the template and Foundry handles the rest.

The deployment is reachable through the unified Foundry endpoint with the OpenAI SDK — the `model` field takes the deployment name you just created:.

A chat-completions model from the Collection slots into Foundry Agents as an admin-connected model and is callable through the Foundry Responses API with the same OpenAI SDK — same auth, same endpoint, same observability.

Available now in preview: the Hugging Face Collection in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog — thousands of models across every modality, refreshed weekly, deployable onto Foundry Managed Compute with NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, or AMD MI300X accelerators in Global and Data Zone scopes, behind a unified Foundry endpoint with Playground support, first-class Azure Monitor metrics, per-deployment billing tags, and curated runtime upgrades and CVE patching applied automatically to your deployments.

On the roadmap: broader coverage of the Hugging Face ecosystem, additional accelerator families, and Bring Your Own Weights for fine-tuned and proprietary variants deployed through the same templates and governance as Collection models.

In a recent development, hugging Face is where open models are published and discovered. Microsoft Foundry is where enterprises operationalize them — on curated, license-screened, security-screened weights hosted in Azure; on community-built and CVE-scanned runtimes; behind a single endpoint with enterprise identity, networking, observability, and agent integration on top. The breadth of the open-source ecosystem, with the operational layer Microsoft runs underneath. Runtime Verification (RV) tools are used to monitor those systems against formal specifications, receiving monitored events through the pub/sub channel. Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.22231v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 $^\circ$C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 $^\circ$C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 $^\circ$C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 $^\circ$C of margin.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22248v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{OAK-Mind}, a zer\textbf{O}-training, multi-\textbf{A}gent, \textbf{K}nowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.09751v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kernel ridge regression estimates the discount curve as the minimizer of a pricing error plus a penalty given by the norm of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By the representer theorem, the estimate lies in a finite-dimensional affine space that depends only on the kernel and on the cash flow dates of the instruments. We ask when this space is invariant under the risk-neutral drift of the discount curve, so that the estimated curves can be the states of a continuous-time arbitrage-free model. We show that this holds for every grid of cash flow dates if and only if the kernel is of the form $k(x,y)=\e^{b(x+y)}\big(c\,\e^{axy}+1-c\big)$, apart from kernels whose Hilbert space has dimension at most two. For this kernel the estimated curve is an affine combination of flat discount curves, each corresponding to a constant continuously compounded yield. The drift-invariant subspaces correspond to sub-grids of the cash flow dates, and the discounted coefficients have linear risk-neutral dynamics.

We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. #20786. The EPA’s Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn’t Doing Its Job Anymore

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2419 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

The EPA’s Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn’t Doing Its Job Anymore

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government's chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.
  • When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.
  • And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Oklahoma, injured 74 people last November, the federal government's chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.

When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.

And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.

“Ten years ago, it would have gone to all of them,” notes Mark Thomas, a former EPA official who for years managed the airborne detection effort.

The program, known as ASPECT, was designed to respond around the clock to emergencies involving toxic chemicals, oil spills, and radiation. The plane’s sensors could identify chemicals in the air within minutes, giving emergency responders crucial information about the dangers nearby communities face.

For more than two decades, the plane has flown over many of the country’s worst disasters, from Latest Orleans after Hurricane Katrina to the deadly West Fertilizer explosion in Texas to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.

Recent findings suggest that but since early 2021, the single-engine Cessna has responded to just seven emergencies. And former ASPECT scientists say two of those missions—the 2023 train derailment that sent toxic clouds over East Palestine, Ohio, and the 2025 fire at Smitty’s Supply in Louisiana—were badly mismanaged.

At Smitty’s, the EPA declared the air safe, but a former ASPECT scientist later found toxic chemicals the agency had missed. And the agency’s inspector general is now auditing the response to the East Palestine derailment, including the data behind its public assurances about air quality.

In June, the EPA inspector general found a more fundamental problem: The plane could no longer identify chemicals within minutes, as designed. Instead, the data had to be analyzed by hand, a process that takes about a week. That’s far too long to help anyone on the ground who’s deciding whether to evacuate.

The EPA remarked the plane's chemical sensors are wearing out and expects replacements to be working by mid-2027.

According to recent reports, but five people who helped build and run the program told Floodlight that the EPA is fixing the wrong problem. The old sensors still work, they say. What the agency lost, in their view, is the initiative and expertise that made the program a powerful tool when disaster struck. Replacing the old sensors, they warn, could leave the EPA even less capable of detecting hazardous chemicals in an emergency.

“I fear that the public is at risk,” says Robert Kroutil, a longtime ASPECT scientist who helped develop the program and later became a whistleblower. “It’s such an important program, and they've allowed it to waste away to nothing.”.

The EPA did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview or questions about ASPECT’s decline, its handling of emergencies, the replacement of its sensors, and allegations of mismanagement by former program scientists and managers.

The country’s need for a chemical-sensing plane grew from the smoldering, toxic debris in Manhattan on September 11, 2001, when the EPA’s monitoring trucks were stranded on the wrong side of the Hudson River, unable to cross after bridges and tunnels into the city closed.

Kroutil was a program manager for the Department of Defense at the time, leading a research team that had developed the technology that would become ASPECT, short for Airborne Spectral Photometric Environmental Collection Technology.

The military transferred the program to the EPA for use in detecting hazardous chemicals during civilian emergencies.

It became a critical tool for emergency responders over the next 20 years.

For 72 hours after Hurricane Katrina struck, it was the only emergency response aircraft flying over Fresh Orleans, where it helped locate a missing 55-gallon drum of potentially lethal chloroacetic acid.

During the Deepwater Horizon disaster, it became a key tool for tracking oil slicks in the Gulf of Mexico.

And when a fire engulfed 15 massive tanks at a chemical storage terminal east of Houston in 2019, the ASPECT plane helped emergency responders track the plume, which contained the carcinogen benzene.

Richard Lawhorn, an assistant chief with Harris County’s hazardous materials response team in Texas, indicates the plane could detect chemicals at elevations beyond the reach of ground crews and survey a much wider area in a short time. Unlike ground monitors, the plane can scan a swath of air three-quarters of a mile wide, capturing a far broader picture of potential hazards.

“They’re monitoring the products we can’t reach,” he says.

The program’s success lay in its intellectual rigor: Kroutil and the program’s radiological lead held PhDs, as did Mark Thomas, the former EPA official. The team wrote the code, designed the mounts that held gear, and analyzed the raw data themselves.

“We were very, very hands-on and intimately familiar with every part of that aircraft,” notes Thomas, who later went to work for a firm that develops chemical-sensing technology.

The decline began with the departures of key ASPECT personnel during President Donald Trump’s first administration.

As part of an agency reorganization, the EPA told the program’s staff in 2019 that they had to relocate to Texas, where the plane was based, or face termination, documents show.

The mandate was unnecessary, according to Thomas, because the program had been designed for remote operation. Rather than leave his elderly parents in Kansas, he retired. Then, ASPECT’s radiological lead left the division, and the engineer who helped build and manage the plane’s sensors accepted a demotion to stay in Kansas.

According to Kroutil and two of his former colleagues, the EPA then failed to fill those vacancies with scientists who had any experience with airborne chemical detection.

“They lost the institutional knowledge of the program, and quite frankly, lost the momentum of the program,” Thomas says.

During its first two decades, the plane flew almost 80 emergency missions—an average of roughly four a year. In the past five years, however, it has flown an average of just one a year.

In October, hundreds were evacuated—and more than 50 were treated at hospitals—when a 5,500-gallon industrial tank in Toledo, Ohio, leaked glycidyl methacrylate, a chemical used in making plastics that is a probable carcinogen suspected of causing genetic defects. It was one of at least 80 chemical emergencies this year that the plane did not respond to.

The decline comes as accidental chemical releases are becoming more common. The US Chemical Safety Board tracked 133 last year, up from 83 in 2021.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, has proposed rolling back federal safeguards designed to prevent chemical disasters, including requirements for some plants to undergo independent safety audits and provide hazard information to nearby communities.

Recent findings suggest that former ASPECT program managers say they used to actively track chemical emergencies and urge EPA on-scene coordinators—who manage environmental emergencies—to deploy the plane. After they left, that proactive approach vanished: The plane stayed in a Texas hangar until coordinators requested it, they say.

Scott Smith, an independent environmental tester who’s often called on by local communities to investigate chemical contamination after industrial accidents, claims ASPECT could help him target his soil and water testing by mapping the path of chemical plumes. Deployed regularly, he says, the plane could save lives. Instead, “it's being shut down and not used.”.

On February 3, 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train carrying the carcinogen vinyl chloride and other hazardous chemicals derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, near the Pennsylvania border.

As fires from the derailment smoldered, emergency responders feared an explosion—and made the controversial decision to vent and burn five railcars containing vinyl chloride, sending a towering plume over the town.

Recent findings suggest that ASPECT missed the vent-and-burn operation, and its services weren’t requested until more than two days after the initial disaster. Even then, it was used sparingly. Despite the derailment being one of the nation’s worst chemical disasters in years, Kroutil indicates, the plane collected just eight minutes of chemical data when it finally flew over East Palestine on February 7—a fraction of what it typically gathered during an emergency.

Had the plane been deployed earlier—or flown over the site en route to Pittsburgh, the nearest major airport—its thermal detection equipment might have helped determine that the tank cars were not in danger of exploding, Kroutil later stated in an affidavit.

In a recent development, the National Transportation Safety Board concluded that the vent-and-burn operation had been unnecessary. It found no evidence of the dangerous chemical reaction that Norfolk Southern and its contractors stated threatened an explosion. Temperature readings showed the railcars were cooling.

Sources indicate that an EPA inspector general investigation later found a series of errors in the East Palestine response: The agency had poorly documented its procedures and failed to adequately inform emergency responders of the plane’s capabilities. The on-scene coordinator, who didn’t request the plane until two days after the derailment, wrongly believed that ground-level monitoring would provide better data.

Industry observers note that frustrated by how EPA officials were running the program, Kroutil retired. Two of his colleagues also left, further draining the program’s pool of experience and expertise.

On August 22, 2025, a massive explosion ripped through Smitty’s Supply, a facility that blended and packaged oil and other engine lubricants in Roseland, Louisiana.

According to recent reports, less than 4 miles away, Ronnie Polezcek and his family heard something hitting their roof that afternoon. At first, they thought it was raindrops.

But when they walked outside, Polezcek indicates, “It was just like it was raining oil.”.

The dark residue covered the family’s 23-acre farm. Polezcek claims he had to burn his hay, move his cows temporarily to Mississippi, and replace a metal roof that could not be scrubbed clean. Two of his cows miscarried soon afterward, he says, and a veterinarian found arsenic in one of them. Polezcek filed a lawsuit against Smitty’s in September 2025 that has been consolidated into an ongoing class-action case.

Sources indicate that the Smitty’s fire burned for nearly two weeks, sending a huge plume of smoke into the air. Local authorities ordered a 1-mile evacuation around the plant, and the EPA dispatched ASPECT—the plane’s first emergency deployment in 19 months.

The agency didn’t publicly post findings from the ASPECT flights until August 31, nine days after the fire began. Those reports show the air around Smitty’s contained ozone and three other pollutants but at levels far below those considered harmful to human health.

A later analysis of the raw flight data, though, told a very different story.

Sources indicate that working with the Government Accountability Project, a nonprofit that advocates for whistleblowers, Kroutil obtained data from ASPECT’s third flight over the disaster area. He notes it took him weeks to analyze it, doing by hand what the plane’s software was designed to do in minutes.

Sources indicate that kroutil identified high concentrations of the neurotoxicant toluene and the carcinogens trichloroethylene and naphthalene, among other toxic chemicals. He concluded that the levels of toluene were so high, they could have put nearby communities at risk.

Many of the findings also matched what Smith, the independent environmental tester, detected in soil and water after the fire.

The EPA later acknowledged a similar problem, according to records that the Government Accountability Project obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.

It has been revealed that in a May 2026 email, an EPA manager said some target chemicals might have been present in data from the third flight but weren't flagged at the time the data was collected. The manager suggested that deterioration of the aging sensors might have contributed to the failure.

Polezcek believes officials should have evacuated a larger area.

It has been revealed that “I really think it was a pitiful job,” he says. “They just kept saying, ‘There’s nothing to worry about, you’re good to go.’”.

In June, the EPA inspector general confirmed that Kroutil’s warnings were justified: The plane could no longer provide chemical-monitoring data within five minutes.

Instead, scientists had to conduct manual analysis that would take about a week. The EPA also failed to tell on-scene coordinators that the program isn’t working as designed.

In a recent development, EPA officials blamed the delays on old sensors. The agency bypassed competitive bidding to award a Canadian tech giant, Telops, a $1.7 million contract for replacement sensors designed for several applications, including gas detection and mineral mapping. Integrating the latest sensors won’t be complete until “early to mid 2027,” according to the EPA.

In contract documents, the EPA cited peer-reviewed studies showing the Telops sensors had been field-tested and proven. But much of the research on the fresh equipment has focused on tracking methane leaks, not the wide range of toxic chemicals released during complex industrial emergencies.

Five people formerly involved with ASPECT have raised concerns that the latest sensors will be less capable than the old ones at detecting hazardous chemicals during industrial emergencies.

Exosens, the parent company of Telops, told Floodlight that its system and the old one use “different measurement architectures.”.

The newly introduced sensors, it says, can identify hundreds of chemicals and distinguish chemical plumes from surrounding objects. The original infrared sensors, built by the Canadian firm Bomem, were rebuilt multiple times and equipped with new software.

Chris Manning, an infrared spectrometer expert with no ties to Telops, the EPA, or the firm where Thomas now works, says the fresh Telops sensors could complement ASPECT’s older sensors but would be a poor replacement. They are slower, less sensitive, and less suited to moving targets, he says.

“To say, ‘We're just going to replace these other two instruments’ … I mean, that’s ludicrous,” he says.

The old sensors had problems, too. Their artificial intelligence software had not been retrained after an electrical malfunction several years ago, Kroutil and Thomas say. In early 2023, contract scientists with the program presented the EPA with a strategy to retrain the software, emails show. But the EPA never took the required steps, according to Kroutil and Rick Turville, a former ASPECT manager who left the program in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that kroutil and his former colleagues say they have no confidence that the upcoming sensors will fix the problem. They expect the program to deteriorate further.

In the affidavit submitted to the Government Accountability Project, Kroutil offers a dim prognosis: “Unless major changes are made at EPA and with the ASPECT program, it is not going to get any better and EPA will be flying blind.”.

According to recent reports, today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI. Developers can now go from model discovery to hands-on experimentation in SageMaker Studio with a single selection. Whether you fine-tune a foundation model (FM) from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart or deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker Inference endpoint, you can now land directly inside the relevant SageMaker Studio workflow. Your selected model is pre-loaded, and the environment is fully configured and ready to go.

Previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota. For developers who want to iterate quickly, this friction slows down the path from inspiration to experimentation. The integration creates a more direct path from discovery to enterprise deployment.

In a recent development, “At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms. This integration takes that promise the last mile. Going from an open model on Hugging Face straight into SageMaker Studio in a single click, then fine-tuning or deploying it inside your own AWS environment with nothing to wire up, is the kind of experience open models have been missing. Open weights you own, running in the cloud you control. That is exactly the combination our customers have been asking for.”.

— Mark McQuade, Founder and CEO, Arcee AI.

Industry observers note that with the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a newly introduced domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:.

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

New Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. This alleviates the need to manually create and configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies before you can start experimenting. For existing Studio environments, actionable messages with direct links to documentation guide you through adding these permissions.

Sources indicate that when selecting instance types for deployment or training, the Studio UI now surfaces quota availability directly in the instance selection list. You can immediately see which GPU instance types (G5, G6) are available under your account’s current limits. You don’t need to navigate separately to Service Quotas. If you still need to request a limit increase, you’re redirected directly to the Service Quotas page for the respective instance type.

Let’s walk through the experience of customizing or deploying a model starting from Hugging Face.

On the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

Sources indicate that you’re prompted to sign in to AWS using your existing credentials. If you already have an active console session, this step is skipped automatically. For more information, see Sign in to the AWS Management Console.

You arrive directly on the Model Customization page inside SageMaker Studio with your model pre-selected. Next, configure your fine-tuning parameters such as training data, hyperparameters, and instance type, then submit the customization job.

It has been revealed that alternatively, selecting Deploy on SageMaker AI opens the endpoint deployment page in Studio with the model pre-configured. Select your instance type (quota visibility included), review the settings, and deploy.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

You can try this experience today:.

Industry observers note that the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience minimizes the friction between discovering a model and experimenting with it. By connecting Hugging Face directly to the SageMaker Studio workflows, developers can stay in their flow. There’s no context switching, no manual environment setup, and no permission troubleshooting.

To get started, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page or explore models on Hugging Face and choose Deploy or Customize on SageMaker AI.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22291v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures.
  • Recent findings suggest that the transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning.
  • We have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures. Model authors can automatically leverage their transformers implementations to get ultra fast vLLM inference, for free.

Recent findings suggest that the transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning. It supports 450+ architectures through consistent APIs, and is designed with the main goal that model implementations are self contained and easy to understand. Going through transformers code makes it easy for contributors to learn how an architecture works, and then port it to other frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, MLX, llama.cpp, and many others.

We have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier. A big step in this direction was the integration last year of transformers as a modeling backend in vLLM. This has been allowing model authors to run transformers models (LLMs and VLMs alike) inside vLLM, without having to port anything. Transformers provides the modeling code, and vLLM provides extremely optimized inference techniques such as continuous batching and custom attention kernels.

This integration gets better now 🚀!

We put the transformers modeling backend for vLLM head to head with vLLM's hand written native implementations across three very different Qwen3 models:.

Recent findings suggest that running any* Hugging Face model through the transformers modeling backend is a single flag — --model-impl transformers. It composes with the usual parallelism options, so nothing about your serving setup changes:.

Sources indicate that *Models that use linear attention are not currently supported, but they will be soon! Custom models where the code lives in a Hub repo are unlikely to work as they will not have been written compliantly.

Each model is compared under three conditions that are identical in every way except the code path:.

The full, reproducible runner is available as a gist: benchmark.sh.

According to recent reports, the transformers modeling backend for vLLM used to focus on attention as the bottleneck for inference. By plugging vLLM’s attention implementation at runtime, we could make a transformers model run efficiently inside the vLLM engine. But there are many dimensions to deployments that only a custom port can target to extract maximum inference performance. Parallelization across GPUs, compilation, fused kernels, and many more, all contribute to leveraging your hardware to achieve ultra-fast inference.

When model authors wanted the absolute best performance, they were still writing custom vLLM implementations.

The latest iteration of the transformers modeling backend for vLLM dynamically applies inference specific layer fusions at runtime to match the speed of custom code implementations, for compatible architectures.

It has been revealed that the transformers modeling backend for vLLM now uses torch.fx to perform static analysis on the model’s graph. This process searches for known patterns that can be optimised. After any patterns have been identified, it uses ast (abstract syntax tree) to manipulate the source code and rewrite some of the operations in place.

As shown above, this results in native vLLM inference speed for compatible models, without having to write a single line of code to optimize the model for inference.

We are in the process of writing a detailed blog post to dive deep inside these optimized inference methods and explain in detail how we manipulate the model to adapt to them.

One provenance implication here is that the model definition and the executed inference graph are no longer the same artifact boundary.

If the runtime rewrites model code and replaces modules with fused kernels, deployment evidence probably needs to preserve both the source model identity and the transformation/runtime path.

We establish that this model achieves flocking within finite time and derive a quantitative relationship between the lower bound of flocking time and graph volume. Based on these results, we observe that imposing sufficiently small flocking time induces an increase in network volume, and that larger initial velocity variance requires greater volume under the same time constraint. In our experiments, we trained a transformer-based PPO policy to select network structures at each time step. Under the most stringent time constraint, the maximum average number of connections increased sharply, confirming a threshold effect. The negative correlation between convergence time and average number of connections reflects the theoretical results well. This study provides quantitative evidence for the phenomenon that time constraints induce connection mobilization.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.22080v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.
